en: Śrīḥ!
We pay homage to the illustrious Lord Śiva.
Salutations to Śrī Vedavyāsa, who dwells in the sky of the heart of the illustrious Ānandatīrtha.
The *Śrīyogadīpikā*, composed by the venerable teacher Nārāyaṇapaṇḍitācārya, son of the venerable teacher Trivikramapaṇḍitācārya, the ornament of the assembly of poets.
Having bowed to Viṣṇu, the beloved of Śrī, and to Madhva, the lord of my life, as well as to the gurus and Trivikramārya, this *Yogadīpikā* is composed. (1)
For a person who performs prescribed duties and refrains from prohibited ones, the supreme means of propitiation is devotion; this is the yoga that consists of skill in actions. (2)
Established within me and my limbs, Hari is independent and all-pervading;
that unborn Lord, who is the self-dependent master of all, turns me back according to his own will.
The activities of one's own mind, speech, and body should be regarded as worship of Him;
thinking "these belong to Me," one should remember Hari as both the agent and the intended object.
This yoga, which bestows complete grace from Viṣṇu, grants both worldly bondage and liberation;
how much more so if it consists of Sāṅkhya and is well-practiced by a qualified aspirant?

The father should initiate his own son— who is worthy and devoted to the Lord— into the Smārta rites consisting of the worship of Hari, beginning with the birth-ceremony (jātakarman) and other sacraments.
While he is still a child, his father and other elders who are dear to Hari should instruct him in the practice of devotion,
dharma, vows, and other such duties, according to their ability and as is appropriate.
A twice-born man who honors his guru, whose conduct is pure, who performs his daily rites,
who offers oblations of fuel-wood morning and evening, and who subsists on alms-food, should study the Vedas.
One should thoroughly study the *Śrīmadbhāratatātparyanirṇaya* and other such works; however, one who is well-versed in the training of logic should not do so on days when study is prohibited.
One should abandon prohibited actions and perform those that are prescribed;
one should worship Nṛsiṃha, Kṛṣṇa, and others for the pacification of obstacles to knowledge.
One who possesses devotion from time immemorial toward the Supreme, who is twice-born, free from sin, trained in the method of grammar, has studied the Vedas,
performed great penance, and observes vows, may obtain supreme knowledge from his guru through [the guru’s] grace.

Having heard the Sūtras, the Bhāṣyas, and so forth, one should reflect upon them together with friends; likewise, one may study the Gītā-prakaraṇa and other such works along with their commentaries even during periods when formal study is prohibited.

The preceptor should initiate that beloved of Hari who possesses the requisite purificatory rites (saṃskāras). Being about to initiate him, the supreme teacher [should address] him who has bathed, sipped water for purification, and bowed down.
One should cause [the disciple] to drink the water from the feet of the Supreme Lord with the mantra "tadasya.
Having been initiated, he should fast for the day according to the vows prescribed by the Guru.
Having consumed the five products of the cow three, seven, five, or even ten times,
the Guru should draw a wheel within a lotus on a clean, level, and firm spot.
One should perform the ritual bathing of the jar and other rites for the sake of increasing the presence [of the deity] within Hari;
likewise, one should do so in every way even when portents are observed.
To his left, in a clean place in front of him, he should draw a lotus;
in its center he should fill it with rice, and upon those grains he should spread darbha grass.

There, having smeared the exterior with cow-dung and water, he should place a *kūrca* (bundle of grass) together with unbroken grains (*akṣata*), saying, "May Viṣṇu be pleased with me," and then worship it with flowers and unbroken grains.
Having washed the jar, one should then wrap it with a threefold thread;
one should fumigate it both inside and out, and then place another [vessel] upon the lotus.

Having fashioned a seat (*kūrca*) from twelve, nine, or even three blades of *darbha* grass, and having meditated upon it as being the very essence of Hari’s form, one should tie it and place it upon that [seat].
Then the practitioner, having performed his ablutions, being properly purified and possessing a clean body,
should perform the worship of the self-lamp and the obstructions, and then carry out the worship of the ritual pitcher (kalaśa).
Having first performed the worship of the sacred seat (pīṭha), the wise one should turn the water-pot upright;
he should then place sandalwood, unbroken rice grains, flowers, and gold pieces within it.
On the day, when the waters have been drawn up and purified through a cloth by the presiding priests (mūrtipas),
one should invoke Hari into those waters with the verse addressed to Varuṇa or with the root mantra.
Having placed the tip of the *kūrca* grass into the mouth of the jar,
one should sprinkle oneself there while reciting the root mantra and others, as well as the syllables (*lipi*) in reverse order.
One should stir the water with eight parts of each of the eight fragrant substances:
uśīra, kumuda, māṃsī, kuṣṭha, sandalwood (malayaja), agaru, [elā], and [tagara]. (25)
Hīra, bera, and mura—these are declared to be the eight fragrant substances (gandhāṣṭaka). And in the absence of these perfumes, sandalwood is recommended. 26.
Having prepared a high seat (*kūrca*) there, one should invoke Hari with the root mantra;
likewise, one should offer incense, fragrance, flowers, and unbroken rice grains with palms joined in reverence.
Having directed the power of attraction toward him, one should recite the root mantra thirty times;
at the end of the *tāra* (oṃ), having uttered "O Blessed One," followed by "come hither. (28)
Having said, "I invoke," one should recite the root mantra three times;
then the fourteen seed-syllables, and once again the root mantra should be uttered. (29)
In this manner, as one lamp is lit from another, he should bring forth the expanded form of Viṣṇu from the sun with cupped hands and invoke it into the water.
One should seal the seat with the root mantra using the two thumbs at the base of the two little fingers;
then, one should utter the root mantra for the thorough sealing, as well as the greeting "svāgatam. (31)
Then, having joined the two ring fingers, one should recite "Be firm" (sthiro bhava);
then, having clenched them into fists, one should recite over the thumbs "Be well-restrained" (sanniruddho bhava). || 32 ||
With the root mantra and the *bindu-mudrā*, one should say: "Be present!
Then, having clenched the hands into fists, the two thumbs should be joined together. (33)
Having recited the root mantra once, one should say: "Be established. Having thus honored [the deity], one should perform the pervasive placement (*vyāpakanyāsa*) with the mudrās. || 34 ||
Then, with thirty-six *tālas*, one should assign the root-limbs (*mūlāṅga*) beginning with the root;
having thus performed the invocation (*āvāhana*) and the assignment of the limbs of the *lipis* (*lipyaṅganyāsa*), one should then assign the *lipis* themselves.
Or else, one may practice the hundred arts (kalās) in reverse order, including the stars and the beginning with the letter 'ja';
these are the limbs of the principles (tattvas), consisting of the nature of maintenance, origination, and dissolution.
One should assign the limbs consisting of the syllables of the root mantra to Hari, as well as the ṛṣi and other [limbs], and [the ornaments]:
the discus, conch, mace, lotus, garland, śrīvatsa, and kaustubha.
One should press the crown, the earrings, the yoni, and those two shibhus;
then, having muttered the seed-syllable of the moon-born one, one should remain bowed with palms joined in reverence. (38)
One should ask for forgiveness, saying "Forgive me," and propitiate them, saying "Be gracious.
One should cast leaves of the jackfruit, the holy fig tree, and the mango into the water-pot. || 39 ||
Having placed rice upon a leaf in a cup made of gold, silver, or copper,
one should cover that vessel, together with its fruit, with a cloth.
Having meditated upon the Lord of Śrī, who purifies by his own splendor according to the manner of the ceremonial bath, one should mutter the root mantra a thousand times at most.

Having performed the fivefold offering beginning with *arghya*, one should again, with affection, conclude the worship by means of the full jar (*sampūrṇakalaśa*) and the six [substances] beginning with water.
Having offered oblations as an auxiliary to the *kalaśa*, one should worship the residual drops (*sampāta*) therein;
then, having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the limbs (*aṅga*) there, one should likewise seal the *cakra* and other components with mudrās. || 43 ||
Then, with the Astra-mantra recited three times, one should display the Ari-mudrā. Next, one should worship Viṣṇu in the lotus of the Cakra with wealth accumulated through His power.
There, one should worship the Supreme One, and the guardians of the images (mūrtipās) should perform the fire oblations (homas).
Then, the Guru should sprinkle himself, having been initiated, with water from a sacred bathing place (tīrtha).
One should perform the three claps and so forth, and touch the crown of his head; having recollected the vital air within that, one should meditate upon the Supreme within that.
One should awaken the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) oneself by means of three *prāṇāyāmas* with the *tāra*.
One should dissolve [the elements] through *prāṇāyāmas* consisting of five [syllables], ending with the long vowels and the letter *ja*. 47.
Having recollected that his body was composed of the elements beginning with earth, he [saw] the embodied Brahman situated within it,
burdened by sinful karma and surrounded by hundreds of evildoers.
One should dry up [the body] by means of the expansion of the vital air (vāyu) through the various supports of the organs of action;
having restrained those vital airs with fire, one should burn them away by means of the "Puruṣa" breath.
The Supreme Lord purifies the head with the Varuṇa-mantra by means of the flowing nectars from the moon;
he immerses it into the marrow, which is of the nature of nectar.
One should cause [the disciple] to generate [this state] by distinguishing it through the six qualities, such as knowledge and devotion;
while recollecting the Lord, one should mutter the *tāra* mantra twenty-five times. (51)

Having recollected the forms of the principles (tattvas) by means of the process of emanation, the empowered one [then perceives] that which resides within the body of Brahmā, possessing the radiance of consciousness illuminated like a lamp. 52.
One should contemplate that the Supreme Self creates, through the gateway of the mouth, that which has the appearance of a drop of nectar and is nourished by the true deities. 43.
One should perform five breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas) as they have been described in reverse order;
then [one should meditate upon] Hari, who is endowed with all limbs and flows with nectar.
One should remember that most excellent Gurudeva, who is full of devotion, knowledge, and other virtues;
and with a concentrated mind, having meditated upon Hari, one should perform all the rites such as the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) and the application of sacred ashes (*vilepana*).
Having bowed down and received permission from Hari and his preceptor,
he, with a bundle of kusha grass in hand, should slowly proceed toward the northeast to the bathing pavilion.
Having seen the sun and remembered Hari,
one should sit upon a seat prepared with kuśa grass, rice grains, and unbroken rice (akṣata) within a svastika diagram, with the knees raised.
Then the preceptor should worship the jar with water, perfumes, and other offerings;
having presented the *arghya* for departure and performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) on his limbs, he should slowly lift him up.
One should lead it clockwise, adorned with a parasol;
the noble one should bring that pitcher accompanied by a special musical instrument.
Taking an unblemished vessel at the base [of the image], one should fumigate it with drops from a sprig;
having placed a tuft of grass [upon it], one should bathe it with the waters of the jars while joining the palms in reverence.
The wise one should recite the root mantra and likewise the letters in their natural order;
then, with a concentrated mind, he should meditate upon this form while reciting the Puruṣasūkta.
Having again performed the placement of the limbs (aṅganyāsa), he should touch his heart there;
then, having put on a new garment or one that has been washed, and having sipped water (ācamana), he should remain humble.
Having applied the vertical *puṇḍra* mark and observing silence, he should prostrate before Hari in the pavilion;
the preceptor should then seat him as he bows on the right side.
One should smear him with clarified butter using the remnants of the oblation from the ritual service;
then, having again performed the placement of the syllables (nyāsa) on the limbs and so forth, one should touch him and mutter the mantra.
By means of yoga, one should cause the Lord of Śrī to shine forth within his heart;
then, having dismissed the multitude with the approval of those dear to Hari.
To one who has performed the *urdhvajānu* posture, with hands joined in the *añjali* mudrā and the topknot (*kūrca*) shimmering,
he should cause him to hear the supreme reality as well as the other root mantras.
Three, four, or five times, as appropriate and according to the rule,
the Guru should place his hand, which consists of the Vedas, upon the disciple's head.
One should grant devotion, knowledge, and so forth as an offering for the pleasure of Hari;
then the preceptor, together with the image-bearers, should be honored with sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇās).
One should feed the Vaiṣṇavas with food offered to Viṣṇu;
having concluded the worship, one should pray to the Supreme Lord. (69)
For he indeed bestows all fruits and brings about the success of the disciple's ritual actions;
therefore, one should gradually listen to this compendium of the essence of the Tantra with reverence.
One should practice the scripture taught in the Tantra, which illuminates higher knowledge;
one should recite the mantras proclaimed therein and perform meditation upon those deities. (71)
The Supreme Self quickly becomes pleased with that person who has attained perfection in mantra;
such a person is especially worthy of yoga.
Therefore, having been favored by destiny, that happy person should practice yoga. || 73 ||
Thus ends the first chapter of the Yogadīpikā.
The second chapter:
A person intending to practice yoga [should first examine] his own body, senses, and so forth.
One should meditate upon the body, senses, and so forth of Hari as being existence, consciousness, and bliss (saccidānanda). || 1 ||
Then, while performing any action whatsoever, one should unite it with Hari, thinking:
"The Lord, abiding in me, performs this; may I do this for His pleasure. || 2 ||
Or he may wander as a mendicant, studying under a supreme teacher;
otherwise, a wise teacher should cause him to return home.

Having obtained boons from a guru who was satisfied by his service and sacrificial fees, that wise man, having drunk from the nectar-ocean of Sāṅkhya and Yoga, may enter another stage of life (āśrama). || 4 ||
One should worship the Blessed One constantly with the conduct appropriate to one’s own stage of life;
what is the use of that which causes harm by abandoning everything else? (5)
Non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, celibacy, and non-possessiveness;
being pure, ascetic, contented, and devoted to the study of scripture and worshipful vows. (6)

One who possesses great vigor should listen to the true scripture again and again after questioning it; he should deliberate with his friends until there is a complete determination of the scripture in every respect. (7)
Having withdrawn his impurities through breath-control (prāṇāyāma) beginning with the lotus posture,
and meditating on Hari, he should again study the supreme scripture.
One may even teach this to disciples; such is the completeness of worship.
One should be devoted to those who are good and excellent, and affectionate toward those who are good but of lower status.
One should not harbor envy, anger, or malice toward the devotees of Hari,
nor toward those who serve the dust of the feet of the venerable Ānandatīrtha.
One should indeed cultivate delightful devotion, for this is the medicine for worldly existence; how much more so toward those gods who serve the glorious Madhva and his successors? 11.
What more need be said regarding Śrī Madhva’s mastery of speech and the knowledge of the Vedas?
"He who has supreme devotion for the Lord, and for the guru as he does for the Lord... (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.23).
Regarding him, this eternal Śruti declares full bliss:
"Having risen during the Brāhma-muhūrta, one should place Hari, the Self of all, within the heart. (13)
Therefore, having remembered this, one who has gone forth should reflect:
"O Master, I am your eternal servant; what pleasing service may I perform for you? (14)
"O Lord, let there be nothing disagreeable to you; may my mind and so forth never turn away from you.
Having thus entreated the Lord of Ramā, he should constantly perform his ritual duties. (15)
First, one should purify the body for the sake of attaining proximity to the deity;
having gone to the southwestern direction (nairṛtī) on ground that is not in front of cows or other [animals].
Having placed a blade of grass to one side, he should void urine there,
facing north with his head covered by a cloth during the day, or facing south if it is at night.
One should perform *recaka* (exhalation) using a dry, firm staff held in the left hand;
then, having grasped the tip of the *liṅga* with the left hand, one rises up.
Having arrived at a secluded place, one should attend to purification with clay;
for the purpose of removing odor and residue, one should apply it once to the penis and three times to the hand.
One should take clay seven times for the anus, and thirty times each for the hands and the penis;
then one should perform the prescribed cleansing, with clay once on the penis and thirty times [on the hands].
Five times on the left [nostril], ten times on the right for the apāna breath,
seven times on both hands, and then clearly thirty times on the liṅga.
Having washed one part [of the body], he should then put on his garment;
having joyfully washed his feet three times, he should perform twelve mouthfuls of rinsing water (gaṇḍūṣa).
Having sipped water and discarded the remnants of the purification, he should wash that spot;
then, having washed his knees, feet, and hands, as well as his mouth, with pure waters. (23)

Having sipped water (ācamya) and again performed the ritual offering with arghya and other substances, and having sipped water once more, one is said to be "ācānta" (one who has properly sipped). Then, at a distance of four cubits from the water and other materials, the sage should sit facing the east.
Having cleansed his teeth, he should bring water and sprinkle that spot;
the tooth-sticks should be thorny or milky trees, measuring more than a span (prādeśa) in length. (25)
The sinduvāra and other such [twigs] are recommended for cleaning the teeth, while others are prohibited.
This applies when tooth-sticks are unavailable or on days when they are forbidden.
One should clean the teeth with twelve mouthfuls of water or with leaves;
having cleansed the teeth, one should then purify the mouth with gargles.
Having sipped water, one should wash away the clay from the sacred bathing place with both hands;
one should not bathe in the waters of others without having first removed five lumps of earth.

Thus, based on the authority of the Smṛti texts for the purpose of accomplishing the sufficiency of the bath: "Having taken up [the earth], one should smear it upon the body, then in the armpits and the hair-tufts. (29)
One should bow to Kṛṣṇa, Ramā, and one’s gurus while standing on the back of the water;
then, standing in the water up to the navel, one should invoke the sacred fords (tīrthas) with this verse. 30.
And one should cause the water to flow away with the mantra "yad apām," and there,
having meditated upon Hari, one should immerse oneself while reciting the twelve, eight, and six syllables.
Having mentally recited the mantras, one should remember the touching of his feet;
then, with the mantra "May they come," one should pour water three times counter-clockwise (apasavya). || 32 ||
One should throw [the water] for the ancestors, thinking, "May Viṣṇu be pleased.
Having wiped the limbs and sipped water, one should sprinkle oneself with the Āpya mantras. || 33 ||
Having smeared himself with clay as before, he should likewise immerse himself and mutter [the mantra] firmly;
having consecrated himself with the Puṃsūkta, he should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) on both banks of the river.
That which is called the internal bath consists of sipping water (ācamana);
it is performed with the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas, using [mantras] ending in the dative case and containing two vowels.
One should wipe [the face] eighty times with three fingers, touching water twice;
for those two [hands], the mantra is "Athaṛvavedāya namaḥ" while facing the east. (36)
"Another opinion holds that one should say, 'Salutation to Itihāsa and Purāṇa.
Having said, 'Salutation to Agni,' one should wipe the lower part of the face. (37)
Having said, "Salutation to Viṣṇu," one should sprinkle water on the two forefeet;
then, with the ring finger and thumb together, one should touch the two eyes in succession.
He should touch the left shoulder with the index finger, the ear with the [middle] finger, and the left hand with all [the fingers]; he should touch the boundary with the middle finger. || 39 ||

The heart [mantra] consists of all [the syllables]; likewise, Sūrya, Vāyu, the Directions, Vasiṣṭha, Śrī, and the Supreme Self (Parātman), along with their respective locations, constitute the beginning and end of the heart [mantra].
In that regard, mantras are highly praised; this is declared to be the rinsing with mantras.
One who bathes in the water from Viṣṇu’s feet, having wrapped himself in a clean garment, [should perform this]. (41)
Having removed it while the hip is still wet and washed, one should tie it on;
then, having sipped water twice, one should apply the secret marks (puṇḍras). || 42 ||
Or he may perform [the sprinkling] with water on the forehead, the belly, the heart, and the throat;
and on the right side, the root of the arm, and the sides of the neck; and on the left side.
At the base of the spine, on the hump, at the crown of the head, and also at the beginning and end, that twelve-syllable mantra should be placed; others, such as Keśava and the rest, follow.
One should seal the base of both arms with the Sudarśana and Śaṅkha mudrās;
thus pure, having bathed and sipped water, one should remember Hari both externally and internally. (45)
Having offered three handfuls of water, one should recite the Sāvitrī mantra according to one's ability;
then, preceded by the twilight prayers (saṃdhyā) and other rites, one should pay homage to the Supreme Self and the rest. 46.

Having performed three breath-controls (prāṇāyāma), one should perform the ritual placement of the syllables (varṇanyāsa) on the joints of the arms and legs, including their tips, as well as on the navel, heart, and mouth. (47)

Having performed the pervasive placement (*vyāpaka-nyāsa*) with the syllables beginning with *Tārā* (Om), one should perform the placement of the limbs (*aṅga-nyāsa*) and the seers (*ṛṣi*) and so forth, while meditating upon Viṣṇu situated within the solar orb according to the path taught by Madhva. 48.

Remaining silent, one should mutter the Gāyatrī, thinking, "May the Blessed Lord be pleased," in a level, secluded, and pure place, seated upon any of the [prescribed] postures such as the lotus posture (padmāsana). || 49 ||

Facing east with palms joined in reverence, one should remember and sprinkle [the water] first upon the Brahman; then in the middle, upon the right side, and upon the left side, one should remember all the gurus and all the deities. (50)
Having saluted all the gurus at the root with his own heart-mantras and the *satāra* [five-syllable mantra],
the wise one, being duly authorized by them, should perform the ritual placement of the hands (*karanyāsa*).

One should place [the mantras] on the inner and outer sides of the two arms and on the fingers beginning with the little finger by means of the seed-syllables of Tārā and Agni; this is declared to be the ritual placement of the hands (karanyāsa).
With his hand blazing like the fire of Nṛsiṃha, he should perform three claps of the palms;
with the showers of sparks issuing from them, he should burn away all obstacles.
With the mudrā of the manifest weapon, whose blazing flames are fanned by the wind,
he should cause those [obstacles] being consumed to melt away, gradually binding them within the ten directions.
One should fashion a rampart around the fire with one’s own mudrā;
for one seated with the body straight, the Suṣumnā becomes manifest.
At the crown of the head, above the sun, is the Suṣumnā, the lamp of light;
in its center, within the heart-lotus, is the cause of the root-arteries and so forth.
One should remember Nārāyaṇa as one’s own reflection before oneself:
"Though there is a difference between us, you are the original image (bimba) and I am the reflection (pratibimba). 57.
"O Master, you are faultless; please discern my fault; salutations be unto you!
Thus was he entreated by his own servant, who had been chanting with the splendor of his [the Lord's] very sight.
One should thus separate the evil from such a body and sense-faculties;
thereafter, one should perform breath control (prāṇāyāma) with the seed-syllable of Vāyu, remaining immovable.
That [breath] consists of three parts: exhalation (recaka), inhalation (pūraka), and retention (kumbhaka).
These two, occurring through the right and left nostrils respectively, constitute the initial stages of the breath-holding process.
Inhalation should be twice the duration of exhalation, or retention should be three times that of inhalation;
then, by the awakening of the *mūlaśakti* through the forceful expansion of the inhalation, there occurs the expulsion from the mouth.
The wind, joined with the Kaumbhaka breath-control, strikes away evil;
by means of that yoga, one becomes purified as one wanders here and there.
The individual soul (jīva), possessing both the gross and subtle bodies, reaches the end of the entire body through the winds of the breath that extend by striking against the air. 63.
By the flames of the fire of Nṛsiṃha residing in the heart-lotus, that evil is consumed;
when this [body], along with its attachments, has been exhaled in the form of ashes by the wind. 64.
The body and the embodied soul shall both become as stainless as gold and free from all distress;
nectar flows from the perspiring moon situated within the heart-lotus, acting like a cooling breeze.
Flowing forth, it inundates him throughout his entire body.
One should designate the limbs as being beyond the *aṅga-mantras* used for the ritual placement (*aṅganyāsa*) upon the limbs. 66.
The heart, the head, as well as the crest, the armor, and the weapons— these,
along with their respective locations and the suffixes *namaḥ*, *svāhā*, *vaṣaṭ*, *huṃ*, *phaṭ*, and *para*, [constitute the six limbs].
Of the six limbs, however, the locations for placement are to be known as: from the two eyes with "vauṣaṭ," and before that, from the weapon-mantra (astra) with the heart and the other [limbs]. (68)
The armor (*kavaca*) pervades the body, and the weapon (*astra*) mantra should be placed beginning with *tāla*.
Then one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) of the seers (*ṛṣi*) and the others upon the head, the speech, and likewise the heart. (69)
"This seer, this meter, and likewise this deity," and the five vyāhṛtis along with the satyas, preceded by the seers of the limbs of the syllables (lipi). || 70 ||
One should assign the Inner Controller (Antaryāmin) and the Supreme Self (Paramātman) to this [Gāyatrī];
and one should assign the syllables of the Lipi together with the stars around the forehead and the face.
In the eyes, tears, nose, cheeks, lips, head, and mouth; in the joints of the arms and feet, including their tips; and in the sides, the back, the navel, and the groin—72.
Here in the heart, one should perform the placement (nyāsa) with the syllables, having meditated upon Viṣṇu in the form of Aja and others, as Prāṇa, Mahāprāṇa, and Nṛsiṃha. Thus [it is said]. (73)
One should perform three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas) and recite the root mantra one hundred and eight times,
[visualizing] with sparks accompanied by thousands of days of the enraged Great Hero.

One should first place the limbs and other parts, beginning with the Ṛṣis and ending with the Dvira, on the left foot and so forth, on the toes beginning with the little toe, and on the thighs and arms. (75)
One should place the principles (tattvas) there in the heart, as well as the eleven supreme ones;
their performance is this "taking away" (hṛti), and their creation is by way of reverse order.
One should place [the mantras] while remaining in the state of both reverse and direct order, from the highest to the lowest;
the pervasive placement (vyāpakanyāsa) of these should be performed with the root mantra at every interval.

The placement of the syllables of the root mantra (mūlamantra) should be performed in sequence upon the feet, knees, navel, heart, face, nose, and eyes, interspersed with the pervasive placement (vyāpaka).
The placement [of the letters] proceeds in reverse order from the locations of emanation as well as maintenance;
beginning with the feet and having the heart as its limit, it follows the sequence of the ritual procedure starting from above that.
One should place the limbs and other parts as prescribed by the *tatva-mantra*, and also those of the root mantra (*mūla-mantra*);
meditating on Nārāyaṇa in the heart, one should seal the body with the discus and other [emblems] using the appropriate mudrās. || 80 ||
When no specific mantra is prescribed, the root-mantra (mūlamantra) is recommended;
it is certain that among all mantras, the syllable *tāra* (oṃ) is their fundamental basis even when not explicitly mentioned. 81.

With a concentrated mind, having joined his palms in the *añjali* gesture for a long duration, he should recite the root mantra three hundred and eight times while remembering Nārāyaṇa; or even six hundred times, thinking, "O Lord, may You be drunk [by me].
Having meditated upon the Supreme within his own body, he should perform the *cakra-mudrā* and other rites.
Having performed the placement of the limbs (*aṅga-nyāsa*) and so forth, and having practiced breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), one should conclude the worship.
All the mantras for the placements and other rites have been clearly shown by the gurus. (84)

Thus it is declared that the practitioner (mantrin), being well-pleased and possessed of great devotion, should cause the Supreme Being to revolve after having bowed to the God, the gods, and the gurus. (85)
One should listen to the Vedānta together with one’s friends and perform reflection upon it;
having gained insight into the Upanishads, one should joyfully listen to the commentaries.
The learned man should recite the Bhāgavata, along with its definitive conclusions, even during a period of suspension from study;
and he, thus performing the hearing and reflection according to his capacity, [attains the goal].
Remaining steadfast in the rules prescribed by him, he should perform service to the teacher;
having mastered the scriptures, he should explain them to his disciples for the pleasure of Hari. (88)
One should repeatedly question wise men who are the best among the devotees of the Lord regarding the demonstration of the falsity of conduct, teachers, the Vedas, and so forth. (89)
One should tirelessly refute heresy and the doctrine of illusion through reasoning;
one should not engage in disparagement of others and should remain equanimous toward all things. 90.
Thinking thus, what wise person would accept excrement and such?
Having bathed and sipped water for ease, one should perform the midday rites.
The householder should perform the libation for Īśa, the gods, and others, as well as the study of the Vedas and the offering of water.
Thus ends the second chapter of the Yogadīpikā.
Now begins the third chapter:
Then that practitioner of mantras, having sipped water for purification, sat down before Viṣṇu.
One should perform self-worship within the heart using other flowers that have no scent.

In the *brahmarandhra* within the *suṣumnā*, possessing the luster of the rays of the *suṣumnā*, one should worship the deities of the seat and so forth; in the center, one should worship the Root Mantra (*mūla*).
On the right side, all the deities are to be worshipped along with the gurus;
on the left, however, are all the gurus, and on the right, those of Harimedhas.
In the center, all the deities of the sacred seats (pīṭhas) are likewise to be worshipped;
Ananta, the soul of the Yoga-seat, and those mantras themselves, each by half.

Having honored him who is seated upon a lotus-throne in the heart, with a radiance blazing like the rising sun, one should worship him with offerings of water for the hands and feet, and with unguents, incense, and flowers.
One should worship Śrī, Bhū, Vāsudeva, Ananta, Indra, and the other surrounding deities; then, having offered incense and lamps, one should worship them three times with flowers.
One should offer the food offering (naivedya) to Viṣṇu, who is accompanied by his glorious retinue, with streams of nectar dripping from the lunar orb in the sky of consciousness.
One should perform the worship of mutual affection three times with flowers, as well as with incense and other offerings using the appropriate mudrās;
then, having again offered handfuls of flowers three times each, one should propitiate [the deity].
Having offered three handfuls of flowers, one should propitiate Viṣṇu mentally;
likewise, if outside, one should [offer them] to Viṣṇu and the deities of the pedestal in front.
As before, one should worship the gods, the guru, and the others with the four mantras;
provided they are situated upon the feet of the pedestal located in the corners starting from the southeast.
Vipaścit, Garuḍa, Vyāsa, Durgā, and Sarasvatī;
then Dharma, Jñāna, Vairāgya, and Aiśvarya. || 11 ||
One should place the dharmas and other [qualities] situated upon its head in the east and other directions according to their respective fruits;
in the center, one should place the foundational power (ādhāra-śakti) of the Supreme Person (parama-puruṣa).
Kūrma and Ananta, the Earth, and above that the Ocean of Milk; likewise Śvetadvīpa, the jeweled pavilion, and the lotus itself.
This [is] the mantra-sun and moon, and indeed the maṇḍala;
likewise *saṃ* is *sattva*, *raṃ* is *rajas*, and *taṃ* is *tamas*, beyond which [lies the supreme]. 14.
One should worship the nine Śaktis—Ātmā, Antarātman, Paramātman, Jñānātman, and Vimalā and the others—in the eight directions and in the center. (15)
Vimalā, Utkarṣaṇī, Jñānā, Kriyā, and likewise Yogā; Prahvī, Satyā, as well as Īśānā and Anugrahā—these are the nine Śaktis. || 16 ||
These mantras, beginning with Tārā and ending with Nantā, are self-manifested;
one should worship them in the center with the words, "Salutation to all the deities of the sacred seats (pīṭha). (17)
Furthermore, having worshipped the seat with the mantra, "Salutation to the infinite self of the Yoga-pīṭha," [he should worship] Keśava seated there.
Desiring to cause [the deity] to blossom, one should offer a handful of flowers with the root mantra;
one should perform the pervasive placement (*vyāpaka*) with the root mantra, and the *tāla* and other gestures as previously described. (19)

Having worshipped with the root-mantra and a flower, and having offered the *arghya* with pure water, one should say, "This *arghya* is appropriate"; for the *pādya* and other offerings, it is exactly the same.
The lotus-seat, water for sipping, the honey-mixture,
and then again water for sipping— these five precede the ritual bath.
In the same manner, having offered a bath, as well as clothing and ornaments, a sacred thread, followed again by water for sipping (ācamana) and a seat; || 22 ||
One should offer water with the tip of a flower, and likewise perfume three times each, or even with the tip of a *kūrca* grass-bundle, while remembering Śrīpati during those respective rites. (23)

Rising with a luster rivaling the jewel of the sky, embraced by the vine-like arms of the Earth who is like a lotus, this Nārāyaṇa of lovely form is worthy of being adorned by ornaments that themselves possess great splendor. 24.

May the illustrious Lord Madhva, who possesses perfect knowledge of happiness free from all defects, who holds the mace, lotus, and conch, and who is worthy of being worshipped with devotion by Brahmā and the other gods, turn his gaze toward us. 25.
Thus, meditating upon Nārāyaṇa, one should offer eighteen handfuls of water, sandalwood, and betel leaves with the root mantra.
Then, one should place Śrī and Bhū on the left and right [sides] of Hari;
the limbs (aṅgas) in the cardinal directions, the fifth [limb] in the corners, and again outside of that.

One should worship Vāsudeva and the others in the cardinal directions, Keśava and the others in the zodiac signs beginning with Aries, and then Matsya and the others; this constitutes the outer enclosure.
There, Ananta is the penultimate [deity], while Viśvarūpa is said to be the last.
Outside of that, one should worship Brahmā at the back and Ananta on the left side.
One should worship Vāyu in the east and Garuḍa and Rudra to the south;
likewise, one should worship Vāruṇī, Gāyatrī, and Bhāratī to his left.
One should meditate upon the golden-winged Garuḍa there, and within him, one should remember Hari;
outside of that, Indra, Agni, Yama, and Nairṛti are to be worshipped in the ten directions.
One should recite the mantras for Varuṇa, Vāyu, Soma, Īśāna, Ananta, and Brahmā, as well as Tārā and the others, which are themselves the designations; one should utter them above that.
Suratejas, Preta, Rakṣas, Jalaprāṇa, Nakṣatra, Vidyā, Nāga, and Loka—each of these consists of exactly one [pada]. (33)
Having thus stated the presiding deities and the attendants of Viṣṇu mentioned therein, their mantras end with "namaḥ"; hereafter follows this ritual procedure.
One should worship Mahālakṣmī and Hari above with flowers;
having sounded the bell, one should also offer incense and light the lamp. || 35 ||

Again, one should worship three times with flowers; on Mount Ruru, one should unite one's own [mantras] with flowers. Having smeared the sacrificial ground (sthaṇḍila) situated in front, one should cause the offering to dwell there.
One should mix this entire portion along with its division with ghee;
then, one should divide it into a consecrated vessel for the purpose of the oblation according to the prescribed portions.
Having spread clarified butter with the *purājya* mantras, one should sprinkle it from the base using the *tīrtha*;
one should also display the *girimudrā*, the *padmamudrā*, and the *saurabhīmudrā*.
The wise practitioner should visualize the nectar dripping down from the fragrant ground;
having offered the oblation with the root mantra, he should recite it at least eight times.
One should sprinkle water with the Satya-mantra and mutter the Mūla-mantra;
wherever a specific mantra is not specified, the Mūla-mantra is prescribed there.
Nowhere among the rites of worship and the like is there any action performed without mantras.
One should offer the "under-layer" (upastaraṇa) of nectar and worship [the deity] once with the root mantra.
Having said, "Be pleased," one should slowly recite "To Prāṇa, Svāhā!
and so forth, while touching the fingers beginning with the thumb, [identifying] the deities of the vital breaths and the rest. (42)
"All this, consisting of nectar, is consumed by the Lord;
it is impelled by the deities and presented in the vessel of the lunar orb. (43)
Having thus recollected, one should rotate the wheel-mudrā with the root mantra;
then, having smeared the sacrificial mound, one should invoke the fire from the southeast.
One should cast [the fuel] with the mantra "indhāna edhi," kindle it with "uddīpyasva," perform the sweeping and other rites, and worship the deities of the seat (pīṭhadevatāḥ). || 45 ||
One should cause the seven-tongued fire to bloom with the seed-syllables of Jātavedas;
then, one should invoke Viṣṇu therein by means of the previously mentioned path.
Having honored [the deity] with "Welcome" and other [greetings], one should deposit the entire [mantra], not the partless [essence].
Having worshipped with flowers and performed the circumambulation with fire, [one offers] the oblation soaked in ghee.

Having offered oblations with the *vyāhṛtis* to the deities of the seat (*pīṭha*), then with the root mantra to the aforementioned deities of the enclosures (*āvaraṇa*), and then while properly meditating upon Hari; 48.
A householder should perform the Vaiśvadeva rite and offer an oblation (bali) to Hari upon the ground;
having worshipped with flowers and offered the arghya water, he should perform the ritual placement of mantras on the limbs (aṅganyāsa). || 49 ||
Having uttered the root mantra, one should cause [the deity] to depart with the words, "O Blessed One, go, go!
and having said, "I dismiss you," one should recite the root mantra once again. || 50 ||
Having invoked [the deity], one should arrange the limbs; one should first flow [the water] and then collect it together.
Then, having bowed and remembered that which has been offered, one should indeed worship Hari. 51.
Having sprinkled water with the root mantra, one should say, "This is the lid.
Having offered this to Viśvakena, one should dismiss the food offering (naivedya) from us.
Having purified the ground, one should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) with the root mantra;
likewise, one should provide mouth-freshener, betel, collyrium, and a mirror. 53.
One should again offer a fly-whisk, sandals, and an umbrella, as with the *arghya* and other offerings;
then, for the sake of generating affection, one should present three handfuls of flowers.
One should arrange [the deities] from one's own station into their respective places, as if from one lamp to another;
one should incense them, illuminate them with flowers, and worship them three times again.
One should pay homage to Nārāyaṇa with hymns of praise beginning with "jitantē" and so forth;
having joined one's hands in a long añjali gesture and sat down, one should worship Him three times.
With a concentrated mind, one should offer the *arghya* and then perform the dedication (*brahmārpaṇa*).
Having consecrated the remainder of the water as a sacred bathing place (*tīrtha*), one should sprinkle those auspicious waters upon one's own limbs.
One should give sacred waters to the devotees and carry the remains of the offerings (nirmālya) upon one's head;
having placed the limbs of Hari upon oneself, one should then again place one's own limbs and so forth [upon the deity].
One should perform three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas) and repeatedly seek [the deity's] grace;
having first touched the remains of offerings (nirmālya) that are unfit for worship and the like, one should then touch water.
Having recognized each of the thirty-two offenses, one should avoid them;
these include eating, drinking, performing worship, using a tooth-stick, and approaching [the deity] while impure.
After sexual intercourse, worship; upon seeing a corpse, approaching it;
during another period of worship, the discharge of urine and feces, and speaking with tears. (61)

The acquisition of blue garments, the attainment of royal food, and the arrival of [a superior] state; even for one who serves, there is the possibility of becoming angry despite the performance of ritual ablutions.
Worship with flowers grown from unsuitable places, wearing a red loincloth, performing the ritual acts of Hari while dressed in black garments, and even touching [the deity] in the dark; 63.
Following after sensual desires, wearing black garments, shaking off dust from one's clothes, touching a dog, eating the flesh of a boar, and likewise eating web-footed birds. (64)
The *upasarpa* consists of touching the altar (*citi*) while reciting the *piṅgala* [hymn];
the *upasattu* consists of eating oil-cake; and the *potrimāṃsa-upahāra* consists of the offering of the flesh of a young camel. || 65 ||

For one who has approached [the teacher], there is the drinking of intoxicants, the eating of safflower petals, the taking of another's upper garment, and the non-provision of collyrium and other such items. || 66 ||
The offering of incense when flowers are not available; sandals for one who steals turmeric;
the attainment of wealth by one who destroys a drum; and the honoring of one whose food is undigested. || 67 ||
These thirty-two offenses, which bring about great faults,
were declared by the powerful Viṣṇu in the form of a boar to Vasundharā.
"Some, skilled in knowledge and discernment, worship through their very states of being;
others, without causing injury, offer flowers with the intellect or present them with the *praṇava*. (69)
"Or the ascetic [should meditate on] Brahman whose essence is Vāsudeva by means of the root mantra"—since this is stated even in the *Vyāsasmṛti*, it is also described in the *Mahābhārata*. (70)
I propitiate Hari, who resembles a jewel, residing within the lotus of the heart in the city of the body's reflection;
I worship Him with the eightfold flowers of my devotion, consecrated by the pure water of the river of faith. (71)
Thus, having analyzed the "flower" spoken of in the Vāk, it is stated in another passage:
"Non-violence is the first flower; the restraint of the senses is a flower. (72)
Among all flowers, compassion for all beings is distinguished; the flower of patience, the flower of knowledge, the flower of austerity, and the flower of meditation as the seventh. (73)
"And truth is indeed the eighth flower; by these, Keśava is pleased.
Thus, the eight flowers of disposition have been distinguished in another [set of] verses. (74)
Even if they are ignorant or powerless, they should perform worship with water;
having thus worshipped Govinda along with the guests who have arrived, [they should proceed]. (75)
One should neither eat nor give anything without first offering it;
furthermore, one should practice the scriptures again and never abandon them. (76)
One should begin the subsequent twilight rite when the sun has half-set;
meditating for one or two muhūrtas, one should chant the mantras of Brahman.
Or, for the sake of pleasing Hari, one may offer eighty portions of pure food;
and one should approach one's wife during her fertile period, but never on a forbidden day. (78)

On the anniversary of one's parents' death, or especially on a day sacred to Viṣṇu, or even on the days preceding or following it, one who engages in sexual intercourse becomes a slayer of his ancestors.

A wise man should not engage in sexual intercourse on the fifteenth or fourteenth day of the lunar fortnight, during the Śravaṇa asterism, at the sun’s transit (saṅkrānti), on his own birth-day, or during the Vyatīpāta yoga.
A sage, wearing a white garment and facing the northern direction, should perform sexual union;
this sacrifice is named Vāmadevya, consisting of copulation as worship of Hari.

Then, having sipped water and bathed mentally while the Supreme Self resides within the channels, one should meditate on the unity of the universe and so forth, and reflect: "I shall become fully accomplished. (82)
"May that Supreme Puruṣa, who is beyond both inhalation and exhalation, be well-pleased with me as I worship him through the yoga of excellence. (83)
Purity, contentment, and breath-control are limbs of dharma, as are non-possessiveness, non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, celibacy, and austerity. (84)
Contentment, sacrifices and other such duties, the study of sacred texts, the worship of Hari, as well as concentration, hearing, reflection, and meditation; (85)
Concentration, the exposition of the Upanishads, and devotion—
these should be practiced especially in successive order.
If ease is desired, one should practice hearing [the scriptures] and so forth;
if one desires even greater ease than that, a man should adopt the life of a wandering mendicant.
No impurity ever exists anywhere on account of hearing [the scriptures] and so forth;
one should especially observe the Nārāyaṇa-eleventh-day vow (nārāyaṇī-ekādaśī-vrata).
Thus ends the third chapter of the Yogadīpikā.
The fourth chapter:
[Salutation] to the one whose lotus-feet are the crest-jewel upon the heads of all the gods.
The venerable Madhva, the supreme object of worship, spoke this very same meaning. || 1 ||
"He who, having renounced all actions with a mind focused on the Self, proceeds free from desire and free from the sense of 'mine,' he attains the Supreme; he, O Acyuta, is victorious. (2)

Having remembered Hari and risen, having performed purification according to the rules and cleansed his teeth, he should sip water for purification (ācamana) and perform his bath according to the prescribed injunctions.
Having smeared it with earth taken from a mound, [one should worship] with the twelve, eight, and six syllables;
having immersed it three times, one should sprinkle it again in the same manner with the Āpya-sūkta.
Having smeared himself with clay and immersed himself, he should mutter the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn three times each;
remembering Nārāyaṇa, the supreme creator of all worlds.
Since he was submerged in the waters and raised up by means of the *praṇava*,
one should sprinkle [himself] while remembering Hari residing within one's own body, reciting the *Puruṣasūkta*.
Having stayed for the night, having sipped water (ācamana) and sprinkled himself with water while reciting the mantra,
and having offered a handful of water with the Gāyatrī mantra, he should meditate upon Hari as residing within the sun.

Then, having circumambulated according to the mantra and sipped water for purification (ācamana), he should offer libations to the gods and others, put on his garment, and immediately spread out a cloth.
Having meditated upon Viṣṇu, who resides within the solar orb, one should recite the *tripadī* mantra—
the Goddess consisting of a thousand as the maximum, a hundred as the medium, and ten as the minimum.
One should remain standing until the sun is seen, and thereafter one may sit;
thus one performs the morning twilight devotion while the stars are still visible, and the evening twilight devotion while the sun is present.
One should sit facing north and, remaining silent at all times, perform the recitation (*japa*).

Nārāyaṇa, who dwells within the center of the solar disc, seated upon a lotus throne, adorned with armlets, crocodile-shaped earrings, a crown, and a necklace, possessing a golden body and bearing the conch and discus, is to be meditated upon constantly. (11)
Meditating upon Viṣṇu, who is threefold from the Gāyatrī, one should mutter the eight-syllabled mantra, having prostrated before the gods, the Brahmins, the gurus, and the attendants of Hari. (12)
Having remembered Viṣṇu, the supreme among all, one should worship Hari through the private recitation of scripture;
or one should perform worship through meditation and the study of sacred texts, as appropriate.
Having accomplished the means for sacrifice according to the Dharma and in accordance with the prescribed rules,
one should bathe and worship Viṣṇu by following the path declared in the Vedas and Tantras.

One should daily perform the Vaiśvadeva offering and the bali-oblation, dedicating to Him whatever is sacrificed, given, offered in the fire, performed as austerity, completed as a work of merit, or whatever is dear to oneself. (15)
One should offer one's wife, children, dear ones, and even one's own life to another;
and, preceded by servants and guests, one should offer the remnants of one's meal to the Blessed One. (16)
One should eat while meditating on Viṣṇu residing in the heart, with the mind fixed upon Him;
having sipped water (ācamana) with the root mantra, one should consecrate one's own stomach.
Delighting Puruṣottama by means of diversion through the Vedas and Śāstras, he should pass the remainder of the day and then perform the evening twilight worship as before. || 18 ||
Then, after the Yāma period, one should sleep while meditating upon Janārdana;
likewise, having awakened during the intervening period, one should repeatedly remember Hari.
Whatever one does with body, speech, mind, the senses, intellect, or soul, following its own nature, one should dedicate it all to the Supreme Nārāyaṇa. 20.
There are these two persons in the world: the perishable and the imperishable.
The perishable consists of all beings; the one who stands at the peak (the immutable) is called the imperishable.
But there is another, the Supreme Person, declared to be the Supreme Self;
the imperishable Lord who, having entered the three worlds, sustains them. (22)
Because Hari transcends the perishable and is superior even to the imperishable,
he is therefore celebrated in both the world and the Veda as Puruṣottama, the Supreme Person.
He who, being thus undeluded, knows that Supreme Person—
he, the all-knowing, worships Him with his whole being at all times.
Thus, this most secret teaching was indeed spoken by Him;
having understood this, one becomes wise and forever fulfilled in all duties.
The gods have taken refuge in Rudra; Rudra has taken refuge in Brahmā;
Brahmā is eternally dependent on him, but Hari is not dependent on anything at all.
Those men who constantly follow this doctrine,
being full of faith and free from carping, are liberated from the fear of worldly existence.
But those who, finding fault with this, do not follow that teaching, know them to be deluded regarding all knowledge, their own selves and intellects destroyed. 28.
There are only two types of creation in this world: the divine and the demonic. That which is devoted to the worship of Viṣṇu is divine; that which is the opposite is demonic. (29)
Viṣṇu should be constantly remembered and never forgotten;
all injunctions and prohibitions are merely for the sake of these two. (30)
Even that which is unrighteousness becomes righteousness when performed by devotees of the Lord of the Immobile;
even that which is righteousness becomes sin when it is not performed by the devotees of Hari. (31)
Therefore, one who desires to prosper should become focused on That, devoted to That, sacrificing to That, and offering salutations to That; he should remain eternally established in That. (32)
This is the constant practice for both the householder and the forest-dweller, with the exception of the student (baṭu),
regarding the Vaiśvadeva offering, the bali offering, and the cleaning of the teeth.
In this very way, the ascetic, though always devoid of personal wealth,
should constantly perform his bath with the root mantras as well as the libation (tarpaṇa) for Viṣṇu alone.
Furthermore, there is this distinction: for an ascetic who has renounced all action, there is no offering of water;
indeed, it is ordained that the ascetic performs libations for Hari alone, and not for anyone else. (35)
Having offered oblations into the fire while remembering Viṣṇu, one performs the *samiddhoma* sacrifice;
indeed, Viṣṇu alone is always worshipped by all classes (*varṇas*) and stages of life (*āśramas*).
Rama, Brahma, and the others are indeed his retinue.

One should meditate upon Him—the ancient poet, the ruler, subtler than the subtle, the sustainer of all, whose form is inconceivable, who has the luster of the sun, and who stands beyond darkness. (37)
I know this great Puruṣa, resplendent as the sun, beyond the darkness.
Having fashioned all forms and created names, the Wise One sits calling them forth. 38.
Dhātṛ proclaimed him in the east, and Śakra, the wise one, [proclaimed him] in the four directions.
Knowing him thus, one becomes immortal here; no other path for reaching [the goal] exists. || 39 ||
By the sage Ānandatīrtha, this auspicious summary regarding the subject of right conduct was composed as an extraction from the words of Vyāsa. (40)
May Puruṣottama, whose subtle body is the eternal experience of all auspicious qualities without exception and who is free from every defect, be pleased. 41.
Thus ends the fourth chapter in the *Yogadīpikā*.
The fifth chapter:
On the tenth day, one should avoid enjoyments such as collyrium, ointment, and the like.
One who observes the excellent vow should eat only once a day, avoiding honey, alkaline substances, and salt, and consuming only food that is not cold. || 1 ||
Having risen early the next morning and remembered Hari with devotion, he should resolve:
"Today I shall perform the vow of fasting."
Then, having bathed at the three periods of the day and performed what was prescribed immediately thereafter, one should recite the words of the Vedas and keep a vigil at night.
Having heard or explained something for a short time together with the beloveds of Hari,
one should perform dance, song, and so forth before Viṣṇu.
Then, having bathed during the final watch of the night, one should, with a concentrated mind, recite the root mantra;
thereafter, one should perform the worship of Viṣṇu according to one's ability and the prescribed ritual manual.
Having offered the sacrificial food (naivedya) there, he should bathe the Pauruṣa Caru;
the sage should sit facing east on the southern side of the Lord.
One should cause a pure sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) to be prepared on the ground, measuring at most one arrow’s length;
one should then scratch six lines with a fuel-stick (samidh), extending from west to north.
One should first draw two lines extending eastward, unmixed with those on the southern and northern sides;
likewise, one should sprinkle three lines in the middle, and thereupon establish the fire.
Having taken hold of the two fuel-sticks, he should then place them on the fire; therein the deities are Agni, Soma, Puruṣa, and likewise Agni Sviṣṭakṛt.
Having prepared the rope and bound the sacrificial grass and fuel, he should place them to the north and below;
then, having swept around [the fire] three times, he should spread [the grass] around it starting from the east.
The southern [line] has its root above and its tip below; the northern [line] has its root below and its tip above.
Having sprinkled water around the fire three times, one should place the vessels facing downward to the north of the fire.
In pairs, he brought forth the large and small offering-pots, the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles for the act of cooking,
the *caru* pot, the stirring-spoon, the *prokṣaṇī* vessel, and the distributor.
One should take two pavitras made of kuśa grass, each a span (prādeśa) long, with tips and without internal nodes;
with the thumb and ring finger, one should wipe them three times above the nose.
Having turned the *prokṣaṇī* vessel face upwards, one should place the two *pavitra* strainers therein;
having poured water into it, one should perform the threefold purification (*utpavana*) toward the east using the two *pavitra* strainers.
Grasping the two nostrils separately with the thumb and ring finger, one should perform the purification (utpavana) everywhere with both hands turned upward; this is the established rule.

With those [waters], he should sprinkle [the site] twenty-one times; with those [same waters], holding the hands palm-upward over the strainers, he should touch the vessels held palm-upward and sprinkle the sacrificial fuel as before.
If it should be Brahmā, he should sit down again after moving away from the south;
having placed the *praṇītā* vessel there along with the two strainers (*pavitre*) as before. (17)

Having poured water with both hands, he should lead it forward until it reaches the level of his nose; then, having placed it upon the Kuśa grass to the north of the fire, he should cover it with Kuśa grass as well. 18.
Then he should offer four handfuls of rice for the Puruṣa;
having sprinkled it with the two purifiers, he should cook it on the fire, washing it three times.
Having placed the two strainers (pavitras) in the vessel, one should pour clarified butter (ghṛta) into it. Having cast out the embers toward the north, one should place them outside there. ||20||
Then, having kindled [the fire] with two *darbha* blades, one should cast the tips of the *kuśa* grass that have been washed [into it].
Then, one should perform the circumambulation of the fire three times together with the sacrificial oblation (*havis*).
Having poured out water and moved it toward the north, he should place the embers [back] upon it;
with the mantra "Savituṣṭva," he should perform the purification as before. 22.
Having sprinkled [the materials] twice silently and once with the mantra, he should cast them into the fire;
then, having removed the *praṇītā* water and brought the *barhis* grass to the west.
Having placed that rope at the opening of the fire, one should stretch it out there;
having placed clarified butter there and heated it, one should heat the handful of *darbha* grass, the *sruva*, and the *sruc*.
One should sweep the interior and exterior with a handful of darbha grass;
having sprinkled and heated it, one should again strike it with a handful of grass, and having sprinkled it once more, one should place it in the vessel.
Having poured clarified butter over the cooked oblation with the *sruva* ladle, one should remove it to the north;
having poured butter over it there, one should place it upon the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) to the south of the clarified butter. ||26||
Having remembered, "This belongs to the Person," he should touch it with his hand;
then, having remembered it as consisting of nectar, he should sprinkle it from above. ||27||
One should place the enclosing sticks (paridhis) behind [the fire], to the south and north in sequence;
then, having first remembered the Sun, one should place two fuel-sticks (samidh) above the kindling wood (idhma).
Having completed the sacrifice to the Puruṣa, the wise man should invoke him into the fire;
he should then cast the cord used for taking the fuel-wood into the *praṇītā* water.
Having sprinkled [the oblation] over the *praṇītā* waters, he should then cause this [ladle] to be placed down;
having prepared the man, he should take the fuel with his right hand. (30)

Having uttered the mantra for the oblation, one should offer the well-recited mantra "This [is the victim]," and then perform the two Aghāra libations dedicated to Prajāpati, Vāyu, and the deities of the directions.
One should sprinkle the two eyes with clarified butter using the *sruc* and *sruva* ladles;
one should offer oblations to the eyes with the mantras "Svāhā to Agni" and "To Soma. (32)
Then, from north to south, one should offer oblations in sequence with male [mantras]:
first the clarified butter from the *sruc* ladle, and afterwards, having twice cut off portions of the sacrificial food (*havis*).
Having taken five portions, one should pour clarified butter over the oblation three times;
having poured butter over what has been taken, one should offer it first into the fire.
Pressing the heart with the left hand and holding the oblation with the right hand, the wise man, having recited the mantra, should offer it into the fire at the end of the word "svāhā. ||35||

Having offered clarified butter above with the Sauviṣṭikṛt mantra, one should take a single portion of clarified butter and twice of the sacrificial oblation; here, one should not perform the Āghāra libations.
Having placed [the fuel] in front, one should perform the oblation at the end of the mantra "yad asya...";
having offered the clarified butter within the enclosing sticks, one should pour water from the *sruc* ladle outside. ||37||

Having offered a sacrificial fuel-stick with the Vyāhṛtis recited together, and having performed the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) pertaining to the Sruva ladle, he should then offer oblations to the enclosing sticks (paridhis). ||38||
Then, having untied the rope and sprinkled it, the wise man should cast it into the fire;
having touched water and remembered Hari, he should worship with flowers.
Then, one should offer the Brahman expiation oblations with clarified butter using the "Ayā" and "Idam" mantras, and conclude with the Śukra mantras. 40.
Having brought the *praṇītā* water, one should sprinkle it in the five directions;
and one should offer the southern portion to the devotees of Viṣṇu according to one's capacity.
Then, one should pour water upon the sacrificial grass (barhis) and complete the ritual service;
having offered the remaining oblation of clarified butter to the Puruṣa, one should present it again. 42.
Having offered the presentation to the gurus, he should perform the breaking of the fast with the remaining two;
then, with the great festivals that bring forth the divine play of the glorious Nārāyaṇa. ||43||
One should conclude the remainder of the day with dancing, singing, and circumambulations;
according to the stated method, one should perform the *āyuṣya* oblation during the birth asterism. 44.
With the hymn "pumān muñcāmi," one should worship the two deities Indra and Agni there;
its seer is Prajāpati, it is dedicated to Viṣṇu, it is full of devotion, and it destroys disease. (45)

The meters are Triṣṭubh and Anuṣṭubh; Indra and Agni, the men and lions, have come together for the sake of prosperity for men, strength, and long life. May that Nṛsiṃha be the destroyer of our death. || 46 ||
"One should worship the man-lion (Nṛvājina) residing within the lunar orb with the final Ṛc";
thus say the followers of the Aitareya, while in the Taittirīya [Āraṇyaka], it is specified as follows: 47.
One should pierce the sacrificial mound with fuel-sticks in the center three times, starting from the west;
likewise, three times on the south and three times on the north.
Having sprinkled sand there, one should spread it out on all sides;
in the middle, one should draw lines extending eastward from south to north.
In the middle, there should be three lines facing westward and extending toward the north;
having placed the fire upon *darbha* grass there and kindled that blazing Vasu.
With palms joined and darbha grass in hand, he should stand in attendance, reciting the mantra "juṣṭaḥ".
Having performed the anvādhāna rite, he should lay down the sacrificial grass (barhis), but there should be no binding with a rope.
Having sprinkled water all around, one should strew the sacrificial grass once at the back;
the cleansing of the vessels should take place before the removal of the clarified butter.

The straining of the clarified butter is performed silently; then, having added the supporting fuel and taken the sacrificial wood, one should perform the sprinkling with the verses beginning with "taditaḥ. || 53 ||
One should offer the Āghāra oblation while recollecting Nārāyaṇa, using the syllable *Tāra* (Om) and the mantra:
"To Prajāpati, to Indra, Svāhā! for the two Āghāra offerings.
At the end of the *cakṣuḥ* [section], there are the "Yukta," "Ādyā," and "Mukhyā" [hymns], which are the twelve-day chants (*dvādaśāhavāḥ*).
Then follow the "Yukta," "Vaha," and "Catasraśca" [hymns], and after that, the "Bhadra" Ānuṣṭubh verses. (55)
"Virūpākṣa," "virūpākṣam," and "yātiraścīni padyase";
"saṃrādinyai" and "prasādinyai"—these are said to end with the *vyāhṛtis*. (56)
Then, according to the rule for one's own portion, he should perform the cooked oblation (pakvahoma) twice at the end with the two mantras "puruṣaḥ" and "sata," joined with the Tāra (Oṃ). || 57 ||
One should offer oblations of clarified butter with the mantras beginning with "sahasraśīrṣā" and so forth;
having set aside a portion for the *sviṣṭakṛt* sacrifice, one should sprinkle the sacrificial porridge (*caru*) with the remnants.

Having joined the two mantras "havyavāham" and "sviṣṭam" with the *tāra* (the syllable Om), and having recollected Hari at the end of the word "svāhā," the *sviṣṭakṛt* oblation is prescribed. || 59 ||

Having offered the oblations for the *anuyāja* sacrifices, including those with the full-length cords, he then poured the libations for the *sviṣṭakṛt*— which possesses the characteristics of both the inner and outer enclosing sticks— over those enclosing sticks.

One should offer ninety-four oblations beginning with Jaya, and then, having sprinkled water with the mantras beginning with Aditeya, one should again offer oblations to the enclosing sticks (paridhis).
Having offered the two [portions] in the west, he should then pour out the *praṇītā* water into the fire;
by this method, the wise man should perform the rite for long life. || 62 ||
Brahmā and Nārāyaṇa are of universal form, and beyond them is Lakṣmī; thereafter, the Vasus, Rudras, Ādityas, Maruts, Sādhyas, and Ṛṣis are enumerated.
Yakṣas, Gandharvas, Pitṛs, Viśvedevas, as well as Arbhus, Sarpas, and Aṅgirasas—these are proclaimed to be the deities. || 64 ||
"One should utter 'yo brahma' above and then say 'bhrājamāna';
one should perform the cooked oblation (pakvahoma) ending with svāhā, joined with the Satarudriya. || 65 ||
With these eight ṛg-verses— “dākṣāyaṇyaḥ śriyaṃ devīm,” “eko brahmā,” and “vasūni”— one should offer clarified butter as an oblation for each one individually.

One should sprinkle [the vessel] with a hundred, a hundred, or a thousand drops, while remembering Viṣṇu in each instance; then one should perform the *sviṣṭakṛt* and subsequent rites as before. || 67 ||
Having recited the remainder of the *samyāta* formula, he should instruct the sacrificer;
by consuming that [remnant] together with the *caru*, one attains long life. || 68 ||
Thus ends the fifth chapter of the Śrī Yogadīpikā.
The sixth chapter:
Constantly performing the daily vow for the day [of Viṣṇu] for the sake of the constant pleasure of Viṣṇu.
One should worship Hari in the month of Kārttika, Śrāvaṇa, or Māgha. || 1 ||
On a well-characterized portion of ground, one should have a mandala constructed below;
having discarded the top layer of earth, one should fill it with pure soil.
It was four stories high, measuring six and a half cubits,
adorned with auspicious characteristics, and surrounded by beautiful panels.
Outside the pillars, it should be enclosed by a wall and adorned with four doors;
in its center, one should construct an altar (vedikā) in accordance with the requirements of the maṇḍala.
One should prepare twelve, or twice or thrice that number, of water-vessels that are well-marked, firm, smooth, and slightly elevated in the middle. (5)
Furthermore, they are of three kinds: *pālikās*, *ghaṭikās*, and *śārāvās*.
Among these, the height of the pedestal for the *pālikās* is four finger-breadths.
The circumference of the junction is twice its width, and its height is one finger-breadth;
the height of the vessel above the junction is twenty finger-breadths.
The inner cavity is said to be sixteen finger-breadths in width;
its neck is half that width, and the mouth is sixteen [finger-breadths] in width.
The circular base of the Ghaṭikā-pīṭha is four finger-breadths in width;
its height is measured at two finger-breadths, and the joint is one finger-breadth in elevation.
Itself, however, was sixteen units in height, and its opening was equally wide;
its mouth, moreover, was four finger-breadths in width all around.
There should be four curved parts of that same measurement, which constitute the foot of Hari;
the joints of the pedestal are described as being like those of a shallow bowl or a small water-clock.
The height is twelve finger-breadths, and the cavity is equally wide;
the characteristic of the pedestal for these two is said to be like that of a *pālikā*.
In this manner, the instructor should have *aurapātra* vessels fashioned for Vāyu,
Soma, Īśa, and Śakra, in their respective directions or even in between them.
Not far from the maṇḍala, one should construct a large pavilion;
there, being well-composed, one should make sixty-four squares.
One should make a path between two [rows]; thus there shall be three rows, or perhaps two rows, or even one according to the number of vessels. (15)
Having drawn svastikas in each compartment, one should fill them with powders—
yellow, red, black, and white— for the houses starting from the southeast corner.
From the southeast (Agni) to the northeast (Īśāna), one should scatter grains upon them; upon those grains, together with unbroken rice, one should spread *kuśa* grass along with *kūrca* bundles.
The *pālikās* are in the east and the center; likewise, the *ghaṭikās* are in the west.
The *śarāvās* are in the south and so forth, within the *svastikas* starting from the Vasus.
Having smeared that ground all around with durvā grass, unbroken rice,
and other offerings, one should decorate it and cause a lamp to be lit for as long as the festival lasts.
With soft sand and cow-dung collected by his own disciples, which have been thoroughly purified by experts, he should fill those [vessels] one after another.

The seed-syllables (bījas), purified respectively and individually with water containing hair and other [impurities], with the six-syllable mantra, and with scented water, milk, and water from the night-lotus, should be placed in separate vessels before them.
One should prepare a decoction of mṛdvīkā, yava, niṣpāva, sarṣapa, māṣa, kaṅguka, tila, śāli, śyāmā, rājamāṣa, and khalva. || 22 ||
In front of the *pālikā* vessels and so forth, in separate bowls, are the deities of these seeds: Viṣṇu, Śrī, Brahmā, and Vāyu. (23)
Īśa, Indra, Skanda, Dharma, Arka, Candra, Varīśa, and Vaya;
here [one should meditate upon] Nārāyaṇa, who holds the discus, the mace, and the lotus. 24.
Having propitiated Vighna on the sacrificial ground, the wise one should worship him with lamps and other offerings;
then, having performed the Nāndī-pūjā, he should have the Puṇyāha declaration recited by his own people.
Having had the most excellent of the twice-born recite benedictions, he should also cause them to recite the Vedic study;
having briefly worshipped the deity, he should worship [the deities] within the *pālikā* vessels and other such receptacles.
One should worship the twenty-four forms beginning with Keśava, or even those starting with the twelve-fold Ātman; or indeed, one may worship only the twelve beginning with Keśava.
One should worship Hari, who resides within those deities as the rising moon of nectar within the seed-syllables, by means of their respective mantras individually, using each deity's specific name.
One should simultaneously offer incense, lamps, food offerings, and so forth for them;
and with the root mantra joined with the seed-syllables, one should worship the Moon (Sudhāruci) within the vessel.
Having touched those [substances], one should mutter the Auṣadhī-sūkta while remembering Hari;
then, having caused the auspicious moment to be determined by the best of Brahmins, one should provide the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
Having played musical instruments such as the *śaṅkha* and others, and being prepared with his instruments,
he bowed down and was granted permission by the gods and the most eminent of Brahmins.
"Victory to you, O lotus-eyed one; salutations to you, O creator of the universe!
O Subrahmaṇya, let there be salutation to you; salutations to you, O primordial Puruṣa! (32)
With this mantra, while holding *kūrca* grass in his hand and remembering Hari, he should sow the seeds into the *pālikās* and other vessels according to the previously mentioned sequence.
In the same way, one should sprinkle those [items] with night-water while reciting that mantra;
then, one should encircle them on the outside with a thick, great [mudrā] through the external yoga.
One should worship them three times a day with offerings of water, flowers, food, and so forth;
the Guru, who knows what is deficient or excessive, should sprinkle water while holding the *kūrca* grass-bundle in his hand.
At night, having smeared sacrificial altars (sthaṇḍila) in the eight directions beginning with the east,
one should place darbha grass and a ritual bundle (kūrca) there, facing east, in the proper sequence.

One should offer the bali-oblation on that day with the words "Homage to the bhūtas and grahas," and so forth, followed by those for the ancestors (pitṛs), yakṣas, gandharvas, and brahmās, in their proper order. (37)
Having said, "Obeisance to the planets," and thereafter to Rudra and Viṣṇu,
and having said, "To their attendants," one should scatter the bali offering all around.
It is declared that [the rite] mixed with Bhūtakrūra should last for seven nights;
however, if it exceeds those nights, one should worship only the Vaiṣṇavas.

One should easily apply those various specific qualities to the aspirants (*kūras*) according to their accessibility; it must not be entered by those who are deceitful, nor by the impure, nor by the greedy. (40)
In that well-guarded maṇḍala, let the Vaiṣṇavas sit comfortably,
along with pure Bhāgavatas and twice-born brahmins, for three days prior to the great festival.
One should practice the private recitation of the Vedas with devotion, thinking, "May Śrī Viṣṇu be pleased.
Indeed, the leaves of the Aśvattha, Udumbara, Vaṭa, and Plakṣa trees [are suitable]. (42)
Each measuring one cubit in length and possessing an extent of eight fingers,
with those [sections] being equal in height and width, and having five such staffs, each five cubits long.
One should have tridents half a cubit in length fashioned for the purpose of the arches;
or one should have eight small banners made by skilled craftsmen.
And banners should be fashioned according to their respective specific colors:
red, orange, blue, white, yellow, and another, black.
White and of various colors, with the splendor of many-colored banners,
the Hotṛ priest, leaving the altar, [proceeded] between the Lord of Waters and the Wind-god.
In the pavilion, one should perform the worship of the lamps, the removal of obstacles, and other rites;
there, upon a level spot on the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), one should cast the ritual lines (sūtra).
One should dig that ground to a depth of exactly twenty-four finger-breadths, so that it becomes a square measuring twenty-four finger-breadths on each side.
One should discard that earth from the eastern side, either half of it or a sixth part.
Three girdles (mekhalās) should be made, or only one in the case of a simplified rite.
The first [line] is provided with three fingers from the beginning; the middle one is measured by eight [fingers];
the last is measured by four fingers, situated at a distance of one finger from the excavation.
One should fashion the vulva with a width of four finger-breadths;
it should be twelve finger-breadths wide and fifteen finger-breadths long. 51.
