Within the middle of the pit, where half a finger's breadth has been set down, one should fashion [the shape] rising according to the sequence of the thread;
it should resemble an aśvattha leaf from the front, and one should arrange it for each finger-breadth.
One should construct a square base, elevated by a height measured in finger-breadths equal to the lunar days (tithi),
and provide it with a middle girdle at the entrance of its circumference.
A sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) constructed without the proper characteristics will cause the destruction of the lineage;
therefore, one who is composed should make it perfectly level in every respect according to the prescribed measurements.
One should place sacrificial wooden pegs (śaṅku) here at the corners;
one should fashion the altar (vedi) all around and eight sacrificial pits (kuṇḍa) in the cardinal directions.
It is quadrangular, auspicious in form, resembling a half-moon, situated within a triangle,
circular, hexagonal, lotus-like, and octagonal, extending toward the directions beginning with the northeast.
The characteristics of the square have been declared according to the measurement of the preceptor’s pit;
having made the square the primordial nature (*prakṛti*), one should describe all other [geometrical forms] in every respect.
One should draw the diagonal lines between the first and the western squares;
then, having fixed a thread at their center, one should rotate it from the center outwards.
On the sixth part of the middle line, one should draw [a mark] outward to the east;
there, the wise man should place two lines between the two circles.
Having set aside one finger's breadth of water, one should draw a half-moon;
at the fourth part of the middle line, one should extend it outward toward the east and west.
From the center of that, one should draw lines toward the feet on both sides, and between those two;
thus, by means of these lines, there arises a triangle.
By means of an eighth part of the middle line, one should draw a circular outer circle;
from the middle line, it should extend outward to the west and east by a sixth part.
One should draw two fish-shaped figures from the center toward both sides; one should take threads at those points, and thus the six-cornered *kuṇḍa* is formed.
One should draw lines from the outer corners of the Mitra-portion (the southeast) toward the tips of the subsequent portions in the various directions;
by joining them to one another at those respective points, one should form eight fish-figures (matsyas).

A Vaiṣṇava should construct the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) endowed with these characteristics; the measurements, the depth of the excavation, and other features of these should be like those of the square pit.
Thus ends the sixth chapter in the Yogadīpikā.
The seventh chapter:
The preceptor, having bathed according to the prescribed rules on the eleventh day and having observed his vows, [proceeds].
Having satisfied and worshipped the deities and others, one should perform the consecration of the maṇḍala.
Surrounded by four attendants, dressed in new garments,
well-adorned with ornaments and wearing an upper cloth, one should worship him as he stands facing west.
Permitted by the Brahmins, the presiding priest (samūrtipa) should enter the pavilion;
standing to the west of the altar, he should gaze upon it with the "weapon-vision" (astradṛṣṭi).
One should perform the binding of the directions with three claps of the hands, creating a wall of flames;
then, with palms joined in reverence, one should visualize Indra and the other deities, armed with their weapons, stationed in the various directions.
And one should display the mudrās of the weapons, beginning with the vajra, in their respective places:
the vajra, the śakti, the staff, the sword, the noose, the trident, and likewise the mace.
The trident, the noble lotus, and others, both below and above, as well as the weapons of Indra and the other [deities];
then, having circumambulated [the site], one should go to the southwest of the pavilion.
Seated and recollecting Viṣṇu, one should perform the purification of the body through meditative concentration,
by means of the previously described yoga of the six paths (ṣaḍadhvan).
Then one should anoint oneself and also the deities of the obstacles;
[this should be done] with palāśa branches, darbha grass, arghya water, and accompanied by sahadevī.
Cow dung and water, white mustard seeds,
two handfuls of darbha grass, ten flowers, an excellent thread, darbha grass, blue lotuses, and a collection of medicinal herbs.
One *darbha* root-tip, sandalwood, the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*),
the goddess [Lakṣmī], *dūrvā*, *madhukṛt*, *musalya*, *krāntā*, *harerañjalikārikā*, *lakṣmī*, *bhadrā*, *maghavallikā*, and *sammohinī*— these are the ten flowers.
The image-protectors (mūrtipās) should indeed prepare these items there in front;
the Guru, while recollecting the Discus-weapon, should touch them with the Astra-mantra.
The wise one should sweep the pavilion on all sides, from the southeast to the northeast, using a branch of the Brahma-tree while reciting the Viṣṇu-gāyatrī mantra.
Having cast out the broom and stepped outside, one should touch water from afar;
there, one should skillfully sprinkle cow-dung and water using the seed-syllable of Vāyu (Yam). 13.
One should smear with that seed-syllable and then thoroughly wash both hands,
using white mustard seeds consecrated one hundred times with the weapon-mantra (astramantra).

Having placed three handfuls from the vessel into his cupped palms, he should scatter them with this mantra; then, having performed the triple-snap of the fingers (tālatraya) and other rites, he should purify [the area] with a handful of darbha grass. 15.
Having wiped them clean and placed them in that bowl, one should cast them inside;
then, having touched water with the *Cakra-mantra*, one should employ the *Astra* [mantra] with flowers. || 16 ||
Seated upon the altar, he should display the wheel-mudrā (cakramudrā) in the ten directions beginning with the east,
and touch that spot with two blades of darbha grass.
Recalling the Goddess who reaches down to the netherworld (Āpātāla), he [purified] the earth consisting of the nectar of splendor,
along with the defects residing in each respective principle (tattva), by means of the wind arising from his physical support.
One should dry them up completely by means of breath control (prāṇāyāma) while meditating on the Supreme;
then, one should burn them again with the flames of the Nṛsiṃha-fire arising from Ananta.

One should flood the entire area on all sides with the nectar flowing from the orb of the Lord of Herbs situated upon the earth; thereafter, one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) and the smearing (lepa), and so forth.

Having thus brought that Goddess into his presence, he should worship her with water, scents, flowers, and so forth, according to the sequence of the six paths (ṣaḍadhva), while remaining composed in mind.
Then, one should worship the sacrificial fires consisting of the Ṛgveda and others, beginning with the Āgneya fire;
having enveloped them with cloths, [one should perform the rite] with the Jātavedas mantra and the Agni-mantra from the east and the north.
Then, having exited through the eastern gate together with his assistants and the *mūrtipa* priests,
he should fix the cord at the edge of the *nīpra* (the base) while reciting the weapon-mantra beginning with Īśāna.

In the same manner, one should place a garland of *darbha* grass, starting from the root and ending at the tip, upon a wooden plank at the eastern door; then, with the mantra "devasya tvā," one should install the trident.
One should spread beautiful *aśvattha* shoots upon its board;
one should conceal them with *darbha* grass, or alternatively, one should insert sticks made of *aśvattha* wood.
Having raised it with the words "Arise!", and having established two pits one cubit deep,
he should likewise set up arches (toraṇas) in the same sequence at the other doorways as well.
Suśobhana, Subhadra, Sukarman, and Suhotraka shall be the deities of the archways (toraṇas); for the banners (dhvajās), they shall be Kumuda and the others. || 27 ||
Kumuda, Kumudākṣa, Puṇḍarīka, Vāmana, Śaṅkukarṇa, Sarpanetra, Sumukha, and Supratiṣṭhita. || 28 ||
These should be placed upon the tops of all eight banners, beginning with that of Indra;
one should also fasten flags to the tops of the banners while remembering the Unborn One.
One should offer oblations with water and other substances to the deities of the archways and the banners;
thereafter, recollecting Hari at each respective place while uttering the mantras beginning with "prāk" (east), and so forth.
Having come from within the eastern door, one should fill the jars here;
on both sides of the door are two jars, and on the left is that which consists of the archway (toraṇa).
One should worship those respective deities in the jars while remembering Hari;
likewise, one should fill the jars in sequence at the various doorways as well.
Pūrṇa, Puṣkara, Ānanda, Nandana, Vīrasenaka, Suṣeṇa, Sambhava, and Prabhava are the deities of the gates. || 33 ||
Indra, Yama, Varuṇa, Soma, and other deities, as well as Tārā and others together with their regions, are recorded as the Mantras ending in "namaḥ. (34)
Then, one should sprinkle the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) with the Gāyatrī mantra toward the southeast and other directions;
and one should scatter the vikirā offerings three times with the twelve-syllable vidyā-mantra.
With that very [hand], he should sweep the directions and cast the handful toward the north;
having opened his fist and touched water, he should [offer it] consecrated with a Yajurveda mantra.
One should scatter the tips and roots of darbha grass and sprinkle sandalwood with water;
having placed a lotus in the northeast, one should worship the Lord of the Jar (Kumbheśa) therein.
One should wrap [the vessel] with a pair of garments and worship the deity of the weapon (astradevatā);
one should propitiate the Lord of the Pitcher (kumbheśa) and the water-jar (karkarī) with offerings such as food.
One should cause water from the ritual vessel to flow all around the edge of the wall;
then, for the sake of attaining auspicious success, the Guru himself should worship Kumbheśa.
Having scattered mustard seeds upon the svastika, one should place the water-jar (karkarī).
Having scattered the offerings (vikira) upon the lotus, one should install the Lord of the Jar (kumbheśa) as before. || 40 ||
Then, having filled the water-vessel (karakam) again,
the image-keeper (mūrtipa), having bathed, sipped water, seated himself, and being pure of body, should worship while facing south.
One should perform the consecration of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) in front of the chief deity,
according to the prescribed method, beginning with the three claps of the hands (tāla) and ending with the sprinkling with products of the cow (gavya).
In that place, one should not arrange for directions or time, nor for archways and the like;
rather, the desired task is the protection of those [flowers] strewn and scattered with beautiful blossoms.
In the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), one should draw forty-nine squares for the fuel-sticks (samidh);
there, one should worship the letters beginning with 'a' and ending with 'ha' all around.
One should worship the *lakṣa* and the *tāra* in the center, and the portions of the *tārā* in the girdles;
then one should worship the vowels in the womb, and worship [the consonants] at the front of the final womb.
Having worshipped those respective deities as well as the Vaiṣṇavī Gāyatrī,
and having drawn lines with six tufts of grass (*kūrca*), one should place the yogic seat (*yogaviṣṭara*) there.
One should worship the deities of the pedestal and meditate there upon the Supreme Śrī;
thereafter, one should remember the Supreme Nārāyaṇa sporting with the Goddess.
Having filled a shallow bowl with auspicious, pure embers, [he offered them] to the one whose body is knowledge and bliss by means of her whose body is knowledge and bliss. 48.
"Recalling that 'in her womb Hari's virility [resides],' one should worship;
one should place [the seed] in the sacrificial pit while contemplating, 'Hari has deposited the embryo. (49)
With the mantra "indhe rājā," the wise practitioner should cast in the fuel; he should perform the "mouth of the fire" (agnimukha) according to the method of the Aupatantrika tradition.

After the consecration of the clarified butter (ājya) through the rites of *ullekhana* and so forth, there is an oblation with white [materials]; the *pūrṇāhuti* is performed with them individually and then collectively—this is what is taught in the Tantras.

There is no *praṇītā* water, nor *brahmā*, nor the binding, nor the cooking of the *caru*; there is no fuel-wood, nor the *cakṣus*, nor the *sviṣṭakṛt* and so forth—this is called the *aupatantrika*. || 52 ||
Recalling, "I shall perform the rite of conception (garbhādhāna)," and having offered a flower with the root mantra while joining his palms in reverence, he should meditate upon the deities therein.
One should offer clarified butter with white oblations to those [deities] beginning with Vāsudeva;
the final full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) is for all of them together, and thereafter one should perform the ritual sprinkling (paryukṣaṇa).
Nārāyaṇa, as well as those [forms] beginning with Vāsudeva—the deities of action—one should thus propitiate the fivefold Viṣṇu, saying, "You are my master. (55)
"O Lord, the rite of conception (garbhādhāna) has been performed," thus he should remember with palms joined in reverence.
In this same manner, the rite for the birth of a male child (puṃsavana) and the parting of the hair (sīmantonnayana) should be performed. (56)
Then follows the Viṣṇubali, and after that the birth-rite (jātakarma); then the rite of taking the child out of the house (niṣkramaṇa), and after that the naming ceremony (nāmakaraṇa). || 57 ||
The first feeding of solid food, the tonsure ceremony, and likewise the initiation (upanayana), the four great vows (mahāvrata), marriage, and the distribution of the sacrificial cow. 58.
These sixteen rites, ending with the initiation (*upanayana*), must be performed.
One should offer oblations of clarified butter into these tongues of fire: Kālī, Karālī, Manojavā, Sulohitā, Sudhūmravarṇā, Sphuliṅginī, and Viśvarucī. (59)

Meditating upon Nārāyaṇa, who is established in the fire in His fivefold forms beginning with the Annamaya-kośa, one should offer oblations of clarified butter— the supreme nectar— repeated one hundred and eight times.
One should perform the contemplation that brings about the fullness of nectar-bliss, and offer the full oblation with the left and right hands;
then, having performed the *netra-kṛta-vaśitī* (the eye-consecration) between the two *tāras*, one should recite the *Ānanda-gāyatrī* twice.

Having sprinkled water upon the remainder of the oblation-offering, he should cause a most wonderful lotus-diagram of the Sudarśana to be fashioned upon the altar for the purpose of bringing about the presence of Hari, the Primordial Person.
Thus ends the seventh chapter of the Yogadīpikā.
Now begins the eighth chapter: He shall now describe the mandala, which is a lotus within a circle and situated upon the earth.
With canopies from which garlands of fruits, flowers, and so forth, along with strings of pearls, were suspended. || 1 ||
One should construct a square mandapa measuring four cubits on each side and eight finger-breadths [in height];
having drawn the diagonal lines for its corners, one should then lay down the corner-threads.
One should divide the four arm-threads into three parts each;
one should drop threads upon them running east-west and north-south.
Furthermore, one should double the ear-lines and the intermediate lines within them; those rows should then be tripled.
O wise ones, draw these twenty-four lines of twenty-four squares each for the sake of the paths,
leaving two rows outside.
Having again released two rows, one should make the mouth circular;
there should be one and a half rows for the path, which one should cause to revolve evenly within that.
One should arrange four lotuses from the center of the mandala;
within those, one should draw a circle by [reducing] one-fifth of the interior of the mandala.
One should rotate [the cord] twice within the navel so that three circles are formed.
One should mark the center of the lotus with a circle inside the [outer] circle;
then, on those two circles at the sides, [one should mark] by means of threads extending to the cardinal and intermediate directions.
Upon those sixteen points, one should draw eight lines intersecting one another.
The threads should likewise be twenty-four, arranged in a circular perimeter; one should form the spokes with those threads bound together to one another. (10)

Just as the tip would be on the middle line, so too is the base on the two side-lines; having joined [the points] within the circle from the tip of the spoke-line to the end of the spoke, one should rotate [the compass]. 11.
From the side-lines of the hundred circles, one should determine the beginning and end;
outside the inner circle, one should fashion the zodiacal signs like the tips of petals.
The doors are on the outside of those [walls] in the cardinal directions; on both sides of them are pairs of *śobhā* and *upaśobhā*, and on the sides of these are the corners (*koṇa*).
For the propitiation of Vāsudeva, there should be a lotus with twelve petals;
for the worship of Nārāyaṇa, one with eight petals is appropriate. (14)
There, one should thicken the lines of the threads with white powder;
one should fill the pericarp with yellow powders and the petals with white powders.
The tips of the filaments with red and saffron [pigments], and in between them;
and the tips of the petals with red and saffron [pigments], and in between them. || 16 ||
One should fill the three circles in sequence with white, red, and blue; the spokes and the rim with red, and the space between them with yellow.
Having filled the pathway with saffron, one should draw a creeper there;
its corners with red [pigment] and the doors with white powder. (18)
One should fill the primary and secondary ornaments with red and yellow powders;
likewise, the corners of that lotus-wheel should be filled with black powder.
Having filled the mandala with nine or twelve auspicious measures of rice,
one should spread it out and arrange kusha grass and tufts of hair thereon.
Having placed red ochre there, one should spread out silk cloth and other materials;
the twice-born should perform recitation of the Vedas all around to protect the maṇḍala.
Even before that, on a pure spot to the left of Viṣṇu, one should draw a lotus;
there, being well-composed, one should worship a water-pot as previously described.
When half the night has passed, having bathed, sipped water, and purified his body,
he who has likewise bathed should propitiate that Lord by performing an ablution toward the eastern direction.

Having approached the Lord of Ramā, who is accompanied by Dvārakā and possesses a four-armed form associated with the Śrīlaṅga stone endowed with the twelve excellent marks—one should worship Him; this is the meritorious deed in this world. (24)
There, one should touch Hari, who is seated upon an excellent seat arranged in the form of a svastika,
while reciting the Puruṣasūkta and the root mantra.
To cause that [deity] to blossom, one should then worship with flowers, sandalwood, and other offerings, propitiating the embodiment of consciousness and bliss with the root mantras. (26)
Having first performed the pervasive [rite] as before, one should perform worship in brief with water, scents, flowers, incense, lamps, food offerings, and libations. (27)
Then, having removed the floral remains (nirmālya), one should duly perform the consecration of the person with the root mantras and with the Śruti [text] of Nārāyaṇa.
Having performed the ritual placement of the limbs (nyāsa) and gone there, he should seek out the jar with fragrant flowers;
having offered the water of honor (arghya) for the departure and performed the limb-placement again, he should slowly lift it up.
One should lead him in a clockwise direction, shaded by a parasol;
accompanied by the sound of various musical instruments, one should bring him near the jar.
Having placed an unblemished [flower] upon the head and sprinkled drops from the sprouts as incense,
and having placed a tuft of grass on the head of Hari, one should perform the ritual bathing with the water-pitcher.

The wise one should recite the root mantras in their natural order, as well as the letters of the alphabet and the Puruṣasūkta; he should then meditate on this form as having attained oneness with that [deity].
Then, having performed the ritual placement of the limbs (aṅganyāsa), he should sprinkle himself with the water from his feet;
having wiped himself with the cloth from his body, he should propitiate him within the mandala.
One should embrace [the image] with sandalwood paste moistened with frost-water;
furthermore, one should sprinkle the powder of camphor over the sandalwood. || 34 ||
The five vessels, consecrated with incense and other offerings, should be placed before Hari; having set them down well, one should pour the liquid substances into them.
Then one should fill [the vessel] with water; in the fourth [vessel], one should place curd and honey, as well as white mustard seeds, unbroken rice, the tips of kuśa grass, and sesame seeds.

Barley, incense, fruit, flowers, and other substances for the *arghya* offering are prescribed; while the water for the *pādya* (feet-washing) is desired to consist of *śyāmāka* grain, *dūrvā* grass, lotuses, and *viṣṇukrāntī*.
The water for sipping (ācamanīyaka) consists of cloves, nutmeg, and cardamom;
the water for sipping again is pure water mixed with tulasī. || 38 ||
There should be six vessels for rinsing the mouth, three each for the *arghya* and *pādya*, and one for the *madhuparka*; thus the teachers declare. (39)
Having taken those [flowers], the knower of mantras should recite the root mantra nine times.
Then the preceptor, having sipped water for purification, sits upon a seat of *kuśa* grass.
Having assigned the limbs of the root-mantra, one should begin the worship of Hari;
then, having bathed and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), the officiating priests, their bodies purified, [should proceed].
They should consecrate their respective fire-pits (kuṇḍas) according to the procedure previously described;
meanwhile, the assistant [should take] from the preceptor’s pit using a shallow bowl.
Having first led [the fire] from the Hotṛka fires into the central [fire], he himself should go outside while pure;
having performed the *viharaṇa* (spreading) in the eastern pit, he should then lead it back as before.
Having led the fire that has been carried forth outside, one should carry it southward;
likewise, one should carry it westward and northward, and so on in sequence for the Āgneya and other directions.
Having kindled the fire, they should cause it to blaze up and perform the ritual attendance (upasthāna) and other rites in sequence,
according to the path of the Aitareya and as stated in the Taittirīya.
In their view, no officiating priests (hotṛkas) should perform the cooking of the *caru* in this fire;
rather, the cooked oblation (*pakva-homa*) and other rites are to be performed with an offering prepared outside [the sacred fire].
The preceptor should worship the deities of the pedestal with water, perfumes, and other offerings;
then, causing Hari to blossom, he should present a handful of flowers with the root mantra.
One should perform the pervasion of the *tāla* and so forth as previously described;
then, one should install the hundred *kalās*, beginning with *ajānanda*, in direct order (*anuloma*). 48.
Having worshipped the flower with the root mantra, one should offer well-prepared *arghya*;
at the end, having said "this *arghya*," one should worship the flower once again. (49)
According to this rule, one should pour the water for the feet and the other offerings into their respective vessels:
the *arghya* is the water for sprinkling the face, and the *pādya* is the water for sprinkling the feet.

The third sipping of water (ācānta) has been described; the fourth is the purification of the elements (dhātuprasādana); and the fifth is again the sipping of water for Viṣṇu, who imitates the ways of the world.
Having worshipped the flower by recollecting the bath for the seat of Īśāna, and having offered water with the root mantra, one should say: "This is the bath. || 52 ||
Having again honored the silk garment, he should place it all around Hari;
then, with palms joined in reverence, he should speak these words regarding the cloth in each respective place: || 53 ||
Having propitiated [the deity] with necklaces, garlands, and so forth, one should adorn him with the finest ornaments;
having said, "This is the ornament," one should worship him again with flowers. || 54 ||
One should offer a golden sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) and the respectful water offering (*arghya*) to the Lord of Ramā;
having said, "This is the sacred thread," one should present the water for sipping (*ācamana*). (55)
Having meditated upon Hari, who has been requested by his devotees and is seated upon the yoga-mat, one should propitiate him by saying, "This is your seat. (56)
In all those various specific rites, the root is everywhere consolidated;
and the remembrance of Hari is everywhere consolidated—of this there is no doubt. (57)
Having taken a full handful of flowers, ground with snow-water, camphor, and fragrant liquid, one should properly meditate upon Nārāyaṇa. (58)
As it has been said: meditating upon the Supreme with devotion and with a voice faltering with emotion, one should offer a handful of flowers to Hari while reciting the mantra in a whisper. (59)
In this manner, one should offer handfuls of flowers at least one hundred and eight times,
or else while meditating upon Vāsudeva with the twelve-syllable mantra.
He has the luster of pure crystal and bestows the boons of prosperity and fearlessness; on all sides are the enclosures of Śrī, Bhū, Vāgīśvarī, Aṅga, and the others.
[He should worship] the Lords of the World together with their consorts, their scriptures, their vehicles,
and their retinues, [anointing them] with guggulu, agaru, karpūra, dāruharidrā, uśīra, and clarified butter.
One should burn incense gently and at one's own pace while ringing the bell loudly;
one should light it high with a wick mixed with camphor and clarified butter.
Again, one should thrice anoint [the deity] with flowers and join one's own limbs to the limbs of Hari, just as light is transferred from one lamp to another.
Having smeared the sacrificial ground (sthaṇḍila) in front, one should place the food offering (prāpaṇa) there;
it should be complete, properly portioned, and soaked with molasses and clarified butter.

Then, having divided the offerings for the Vaiśvadeva rite into portions consisting of sweetmeats (modaka), plantains (kādala), and other suitable sweet foods, according to the previously mentioned procedure; 66.
One should offer abundant milk-rice (pāyasa) and other foods to the Lord of Ramā;
then, the officiating priests should invoke the fires in the primary directions.
In succession, one should worship Nārāyaṇa, Vāsudeva, Saṅkarṣaṇa, as well as Pradyumna and Aniruddha, according to their respective directions.
One should worship Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Varāha, and Nārasiṃha in that order;
however, in the worship of Vāsudeva, there is a reversal of the first two.
They say that in that same manner, the dwelling of Vāsudeva should be established;
they should perform the welcoming rites and so forth for Him, as well as the prescribed placement of the letters (lipinyāsa) and other rituals.
Then, having performed worship, they should perform the rites beginning with the fuel-offering (idhma-homa) and ending with the bhavāntika;
thereafter, they should perform the cooked-oblation (pakva-homa) according to the path prescribed in the Avadāna.
With the *tārasaṃhitā* of Viṣṇu, with the *gāyatrī* repeated twice,
and with each respective *gāyatrī* ending in *svāhākāra*, [one should worship] those [deities] possessing the aforementioned characteristics.

Then they should offer oblations of fuel-sticks, clarified butter, and cooked rice, followed by clarified butter, in sequence, one hundred and eight times; or, for ease of performance, even more than that.
Having anointed the fuel-sticks with clarified butter at both their roots and tips, the oblation is prescribed;
they should perform the full offering for each substance, but when there are more than a hundred, it is for every hundred.
With the Gāyatrī mantra of the form previously mentioned, ending with *vauṣaṭ*, [one should offer oblations] produced from Palāśa, Aśvattha, Apāmārga, and Udumbara wood. (76)
Fuel-sticks (samidh) are considered to be produced from khadira, plakṣa, and bilva;
[specifically] those born of palāśa, khadira, aśvattha, plakṣa, nyagrodha, and bilva. || 77 ||
"Audumbara and Kāśmarya" refers to an alternative sequence;
however, Palāśa wood alone is primary for the Mukhyāgni, or indeed it may be those [other woods] everywhere as well. || 78 ||
Some offer nine substances: fuel-sticks, clarified butter, cooked rice, parched grain, mustard seeds, barley, sesame seeds, paddy, and again clarified butter. (79)
They offered clarified butter or sacrificial porridge to their attendants;
and when the cooked oblations were completed, they remembered Hari at each respective stage.
There, one should perform the Vaiśvadeva rite according to the prescribed path;
having performed the Sviṣṭakṛt and other offerings, the officiating priests (hotṛkas) should cause Maheśvara to be removed from the fire.
Thus ends the eighth chapter of the Yogadīpikā.
The ninth chapter:
Then, having gone there, the Guru should perform the rites of offering, dismissal, and so forth.
And [he should offer] mouth-perfumes and other such services according to the same procedure as the *arghya* offering.
A mouth-freshener consisting of a mouthful of camphor mixed with cold water, along with white jujube seeds and powder prepared with snow-water. (2)
Excellent camphor and betel leaf are celebrated as [the second];
the third bath is said to be well-prepared with camphor and other ingredients. (3)
The fourth is known as the bestower of happiness, having the form of a radiant jewel and a mirror;
the fifth is known as the fly-whisk, with a white and smooth jeweled handle.
The sixth [offering] is a sandal, a heap of lotuses and so forth, and jewels and gold;
the seventh is desired as an umbrella covered with fine silk cloth.
Among these, for those that are easily available, a substitute may be used;
if even that is not obtained, there may be water in some cases and flowers in others.
Then, one should cause svastikas to be arranged all around the mandala;
in accordance with the number of vessels, one should place rice and other grains upon them.
The image-maker should worship the deity with offerings such as *arghya* and *naivedya*;
having offered the *bali*, he should take up the night-rotating [vessels] and place the *svastika*.
Meditating upon Hari in His respective forms from Aries to Īśāna,
[one should worship Him] with jasmine, *kunda*, *mandāra*, *yūthikā*, *jāti*, and *campaka* flowers.
With *nandyāvarta*, blue lotuses, white lotuses, *ketakī*, and *girikarṇikā* flowers—
even with these which are easily obtained— one may please [the Lord] through the worship of Kṛṣṇa.
And they should scatter these, especially tulasī leaves, upon the mandala;
then, filled with devotion, they should arrange a row of lamps all around it.
The Vedic scholars should recite their private study (svādhyāya) loudly, briefly, and well;
likewise, others should proclaim the beautiful Gandharva melodies with measured tempos.
Other young brahmins should dance in accordance with various rhythmic beats (tāla), while others should loudly proclaim "Victory! Victory! throughout the ten directions.
The sacrificer, having sipped water for purification and approached from the left side of the Guru,
should stand with palms joined in reverence and recite the mantra at least one hundred times.
Then, having offered a handful of flowers at the feet of the preceptor,
he should again bow down to the Lord Nārāyaṇa and to the Guru.
The Guru should perform the worship for the sake of mutual affection and so forth, as described in detail;
for the purpose of the worship of mutual affection, the Guru should offer three handfuls of flowers.
One should arrange five or seven offerings of incense and lamps there;
again flowers, again the arghya offering, and again a handful of flowers. (17)
Then, one should perform at least eighteen prostrations with all eight limbs,
praising Hari with hymns preceded by the word "Victory" (jitaṃ te).
And one should perform the lustration ceremony for the Lord of Gods with circles of lamps;
then, the musicians should play faultless musical instruments.
Again, having made an offering of a handful of flowers, one should, with a concentrated mind, present the *arghya*;
and one should sprinkle the water for the feet (*pādya*) with fragrant water mixed with unbroken grains of rice.
Then, one should sprinkle oneself and the officiating priest with the remaining water from that [libation], and properly touch water while facing all the devotees of the Lord (bhāgavatas). || 21 ||
Touching the base of the feet of Hari, one should mutter the Puṃsūkta one hundred and eight times; then one should perform the placement (nyāsa) of the root mantra and the limbs.
And one should perform the placement (nyāsa) of the wheel-mudrā and so forth with the root mantra of the Supreme Self;
then, one should ask the deity for forgiveness and propitiate him again and again.
Having performed the placement of the limbs upon one's own body, one should perform three breath-controls (prāṇāyāma);
then, having meditated upon Hari as the agent within the heart, one should worship Him there.
The sacrificer should promptly satisfy the guru with sacrificial fees;
even if he himself is the sacrificer, he should satisfy his own guru with wealth.
One should bestow sacrificial fees upon the Hotṛ and other priests according to one's capacity,
and satisfy the Brāhmaṇas with foods well-offered to Viṣṇu.
Having offered the *prāpaṇa* to the teacher,
one should partake of the communal meal together with the remainder of it, following the twelve rules of conduct.
One should worship the deity daily; however, in that case, there is neither a pavilion nor a mandala.
Due to the lack of convenience, there is no water-pot, no fire-oblation, and no mandala.

One should offer the *arghya* and other items with water, and the food offering (*naivedya*) with flowers as well; there is no need to collect various specific substances or ornaments, as they may not be readily available. (29)
Twenty-eight handfuls of flowers are prescribed, or alternatively twenty-three;
three are for the worship with affection at the beginning, and then three at the end.

Therefore, even if there is to be a concise version, one should perform the fourfold worship beginning with the seat (pīṭha) at the beginning; and at the end, one should perform two, with the root worship being at least eighteen-fold.
The first enclosure consists of Vāsudeva and the others; beyond that, Ananta and the rest;
and Indra and the other [guardians] are to be worshipped—nothing else is intended here because of the brevity [of the ritual]. (32)
In this manner, one should perform the Vaiśvadeva rite and the worship for universal satisfaction once each; if there is a stationary image, one should worship it according to this rule.
First, one should fill the pitchers—either nine or five in number—in their full extent;
first, one should fill the principal one in the pericarp, and then the others.
Then, in the vessels located in the cardinal directions such as the east, and subsequently in those in the intermediate directions such as the southeast,
one should proceed according to the aforementioned sequence upon the lotus and svastika mandala.
One should worship Mūla in the center, and Viśva and the others, as well as Ātman and the others, all around;
some declare that Vāsudeva and the others, or Brahmā and the others, are to be worshipped.
Viṣṇu alone is to be worshipped as "Brahman" by a Brahmin, not the Lotus-born (Brahmā). Having fashioned a four-petaled lotus, if one should fill five [spaces] therein— || 37 ||
One should worship Nārāyaṇa in the center and Vāsudeva and the others around him;
if there is only one [deity], one should properly propitiate them according to the stated method. || 38 ||

Then, if one should be obstructed by water or other impediments at the door of the inner chamber, one should enter within with devotion to Hari and touch His feet while chanting the Tāra-mantra. || 39 ||
Having touched that seat and sat upon it, one should perform the rites of drying and so forth;
then, while recollecting the deities of the seat, one should remain in a place saturated with nectar.
One should worship [the deity] with water, scents, and other offerings while remembering Hari within each of those;
then, having risen, one should worship Viṣṇu, who is of the nature of bliss, seated upon that throne.
Expanding [the deity] by means of the root mantra, one should offer a handful of flowers at the heart;
having performed the pervasion and other rites as before, one should then arrange the arghya and other offerings.
Recalling [the deity] bathed and situated in the northeast, one should propitiate him with a flower;
having performed the bath as prescribed, one should perform all the ritual placements (nyāsa).
The Vaiśvadeva offering is indeed prescribed here outside the inner chamber;
one should present the bali with the remnants in the north-eastern corner using those specific mantras. || 44 ||
Then, having circumambulated and paid homage, the wise one should offer [the oblation];
having obtained permission from those stationed at the door and having sounded the bell, he should enter slowly within.
Having offered that oblation and performed the ritual dismissal (udvāsana), one should conclude the aforementioned worship.
Thus ends the ninth chapter in the Yogadīpikā.
[Now begins] the tenth chapter.

Having brought the deity through the path of the *suṣumṇā* to the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*), one should meditate on him as having emerged from the left nostril and being situated within one's own joined palms. || 1 ||
Having worshipped the image and other objects and offered flowers with the mantra,
one should perform the invocation of the Lord using the eight-syllabled mantra.
Having invoked the deity residing in the heart, one should unite him with the external image;
for all the constituent parts of the image are each composed of immeasurable portions.
One should further meditate upon each individual part, such as the central face and the other portions of the image,
just as they appear in a painting through the inconceivable power of the Lord.
The hands, feet, belly, and other limbs of nine women were fashioned from the body of an elephant;
likewise, the hands and other members of a single statue were made in that same manner.
At the time of worship, until its conclusion, the devotee of Viṣṇu should meditate on another image as having the form of the specific limbs of that [deity]. (6)
Indeed, within the form of the image, one should especially place many [deities] subtler than the subtlest;
and within a complete statue, one should place the various parts and the forms of the inner sanctums.
Likewise, one should meditate upon them as being beyond numbering, in the form of their respective bodies;
for Time is pervaded by them, and the portions of time likewise exist pervading all.
And space is likewise pervaded; all the Vedas are infinite, and their syllables are also infinite, each remaining pervasively present.
And likewise, Nature (prakṛti) is pervaded; indeed, the fifty phonemes are all pervaded and exist there at all times in that very manner.
Having thus meditated upon the Lord of Gods, the Chief Vital Breath (mukhyaprāṇa), the Teacher of the World, even within the various individual parts of the image-forms; 11.
One should meditate upon Mahālakṣmī within all of those, especially in the remaining parts, as being present everywhere in her own essential form.
Having meditated thus, the worshipper should indeed worship that [deity], and thereafter, he should specifically pray for the presence [of the deity] within the form of the image. (13)
All [the incarnations] beginning with Matsya and Kūrma, as well as Keśava and the others;
likewise the five beginning with Kruddholkā, and the nine beginning with Vimala. (14)
Furthermore, he [perceives] Vāsudeva and the others established as the Vyūhas,
as well as those consisting of the Inner Selves (antarātman) of Viśva, Taijasa, Prājña, and Turīya.
He perceived those who were united with the knowledge of the Supreme Self, established everywhere by having expanded themselves,
who were expressible by the fifty letters, and who were unborn, having the form of the letter 'A' and the rest.
He saw hundreds of Nārāyaṇas and others, thousands of Viśvas and others, as well as many others who were designated by such names as "the Supreme" (Para) and so forth. (17)
Having arranged in groups of five all those beginning with Ajita, who possess infinite forms, are endowed with names such as Āra, and extend from the hair-pores to the very ends of the body; || 18 ||
In all cases, beginning with those born from eggs and so forth, [the vital energies] reside fivefold within each of the seventy-two thousand channels in the form of female and male [principles]. (19)
He specifically saw those who were established there, bearing short and long names, singing those [mantras],
possessing the lifespan of a man, existing for a day and night, and consisting of both male and female forms.
He saw seventy-two thousand [sages] stationed there, each arranged in their own groups, who had mastered infinite Vedas and were established in all the Purāṇas and other scriptures. || 21 ||
[He explained] the individual meanings of the words expressed in each chapter of the Śrī Brahmasūtra,
as well as Vāsudeva and the others who are denoted by their respective terms.

Furthermore, one should correctly perceive those manifestations of his, such as Vāsudeva and the others, existing in sixteen ways, present in every sūtra, in every word, and likewise in every syllable. (23)
[This applies] to all things, which are eternally arisen and pervaded by both words and syllables in particular, even though they are infinite in each individual case. (24)
And in all the various parts and sub-parts, as well as in their junctions and so forth, there reside three hundred and sixty [bones] in the form of skeletal structures located within the body. 25.
Likewise, the forms consisting of marrow, as well as those that are all-pervading—thus, there are one hundred and eighty thousand forms of the Supreme Lord. (26)
And those inconceivable portions of Hari and of Ramā as well, who abide in every respect within their knowledge, power, magnanimity, devotion, bliss, and so forth. (27)
Even within the seven surrounding layers of the cosmic egg,
in all the worlds, and upon the surface of the earth with its oceans, [he was present].
[He saw] those residing separately in the seven oceans and the seven continents,
in the nine regions, and on the mountains such as Meru and others.
Furthermore, he beheld the portions of Viṣṇu— namely knowledge, power, bliss, and so forth— pervading and stationed everywhere within all those eggs as well.
Having recognized them as distinct portions of the supreme form consisting of Rāma, Kṛṣṇa, and the others, [he addressed them] in sequence as "Rāma-Rāma," "Rāma-Kṛṣṇa," and "Kṛṣṇa-Rāma. (31)
One should then contemplate all the powers as portions of Hari, and likewise the forms of the single Hari, such as knowledge, bliss, strength, and so forth.
And those who exist individually in the forms of Rāma, Kṛṣṇa, and so forth—namely Jñānarāma, Jñānakṛṣṇa, and Jñānavyāsa, respectively—[should be known]. (33)

Having meditated upon the supreme portions of Viṣṇu residing in Śvetadvīpa and other realms—manifesting as qualities and the possessor of qualities, as actions, parts, and forms—(he should worship them). || 34 ||
[He perceives] those residing within liberated and unliberated living beings, especially within the principles (tattvas),
within the gods who govern them, and within their respective qualities and so forth.
Everywhere at Śrīraṅga and other such places, as well as in the Sāligrāma and other sacred objects, which have been worshipped by the lotus-like hand of the venerable Ānandatīrtha; (36)
Even in the images of Kṛṣṇa, Rāma, Vyāsa, and others,
one should recognize them all as being essentially one, by virtue of their possession of perfect and absolute sovereignty.

And because they possess the power to transcend spatial boundaries, they always remain present within their own worship-images, even while situated in various locations, without ever abandoning their station there.

Having first worshipped that Lord of Ramā—who is full, eternally free from the obstructions of body, time, and so forth, and who is the embodiment of the primordial sound (Svara)—within his own mind; 39.
One should perform the worship properly with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, especially upon the image,
as well as upon all the previously mentioned parts of the statue.
And having meditated upon the presence [of the deity] within all those images and representations, one should pray to the Supreme Self. (41)
In the materials used for worship, such as perfumes, flowers, and the like, as well as in the form of offerings, including various kinds of food and edibles; || 42 ||
Even while standing amidst yak-tail fans, parasols, songs, musical instruments, and the like,
Hari remains established within the worshipable image as the enjoyer of His own essential nature.
Having performed the worship beginning with the ritual adoration (arcā), one should carry out the pūjā according to the prescribed rule.
Hari, the all-pervading Lord, resides within the image as the enjoyer of His own self, yet He is also present within the object of enjoyment.
Viṣṇu resides within the substances such as perfumes and flowers that constitute the offerings of worship; for he is indeed his own self, present within the image being worshipped. (45)
The Supreme Lord should accept [the offerings] in the form of perfumes, flowers, and so forth;
Viṣṇu is present within the worshipper, and Hari is present within the image being worshipped.
In the form of the worshiped and the worshiper, and likewise as the enjoyer and the enjoyed,
Hari alone, the Supreme Lord, sports through his divine play.
Having thus reflected in his mind upon the Lord of the Universe as being everywhere, the worshiper should honor the Lord of the worlds according to his means. (48)
What man on earth could describe the compassion of the Supreme Lord?
There is no effort required for the acquisition of material wealth for the sake of worship. (49)
For even by those possessing nothing, Hari is indeed worshipped without wealth;
for one who is fulfilled by the attainment of his own true nature, devotion alone is the necessary means. 50.
In the image which is a form of mental impression, fashioned through the contemplation of devotion, and endowed with divine ornaments inlaid with many jewels; || 51 ||
Viṣṇu, the Lord of Ramā, remains present and accepts the worship of his devotees;
he partakes of the offerings intended for him, which are the very forms of their latent impressions (vāsanā).
Viṣṇu, whose power is complete, enjoys perfumes, garlands, garments, and the like, as well as various kinds of food and drink, yet these are distinct from external objects of enjoyment.
Various kinds of water and other substances were placed in golden vessels,
each distinct object set within its own separate container.
The Unborn One assumes His own nature as conjoined with each respective form;
thus, by mere consciousness alone, He clearly becomes worshipped. (55)
All the gods, always endowed with their respective forms, abide within all edible substances; indeed, they should offer their own essential natures [into them].
The forms of Mahālakṣmī are present within all edible substances,
possessing their respective shapes and consisting of taste and fragrance.
The unborn one, whose essential nature consists of full enjoyment, again undergoes experiences;
he assumes the essential form of all living beings, beginning with Brahmā.
And as Viṣṇu, the eternal one, he is the enjoyer of their essential bliss.
The continuous flow of manifold bliss belonging to all liberated beings, beginning with Aja. || 59 ||
The god of immeasurable luster enjoys inconceivable objects of enjoyment that have been set free—exceedingly delicious, greatly wondrous, and utterly distinct from the world. (60)
And the nature of Mahālakṣmī is a collection of most wonderful objects of enjoyment;
it is divine, identical with her own essential form, and beyond the reach of mind and speech.
Indeed, as an ocean of bliss, he enjoys the infinite sensory enjoyments;
thus, through mere consciousness alone, he remains eternally delighted. (62)
Indeed, Viṣṇu, who is within the worshipper, the Lord of Śrī, by his own nature and through mere playful sport, worships himself by means of that very substratum.
Viṣṇu is indeed the bestower of fruits to his devotees; of this there is no doubt.
Viṣṇu, residing within the consciousness, [bestows] desire, knowledge, and effort.
Having produced consciousness in sentient beings and bestowed upon them the capacity for independent action,
the Lord of the World indeed makes his own devotee the enjoyer of the fruit.
The wise person should always offer fruits, roots, and other forest-grown items that have come easily, without requiring wealth, and which can be obtained with little effort. (66)
The Lord of the World becomes pleased with him; of this there is no doubt.
For Viṣṇu is compassionate toward his devotees—indeed, what more need be said? (67)
Whoever offers Me with devotion a leaf, a flower, a fruit, or water— that offering made with devotion by one of purified soul, I accept.
Thus, those desiring spiritual welfare should understand that the word of Viṣṇu is indeed true, and that the compassion of Viṣṇu, the Supreme Self, always abides within his devotees. (69)
Whatever food, drink, wealth, and so forth one procures for the sake of maintaining the body's journey, those very things one should set aside for the purpose of worship. (70)
Even in fruits, flowers, and the like, Lord Hari is the supreme; likewise, even in insentient objects, He is the highest.
So too are Mahālakṣmīs, whose essence consists solely of being objects of enjoyment for Him.
And [he saw] the separate [shrines] of the gods, beginning with Brahmā, Īśa, Śakra, and Kāma, as well as those of the qualified [beings] situated down to human level. || 72 ||
The Lord Śrīśa, Pūrṇānanda, who is higher than the highest, partakes of suitable and essential things;
indeed, the god Parānanda enjoys them through the possession of inconceivable sovereignty. (73)
Knowing that the Unborn One accepts for Himself those things enjoyable by human senses which He has Himself seen, one should always offer everything to the Lord of Ramā alone. 74.
The Supreme Lord Viṣṇu, whose form is supreme bliss and who is possessed of great compassion, becomes pleased with those [devotees] who belong to the past and the future. 75.
By offering even once one's collection of karmas, the hosts of gods, wife, children, wealth, and so forth, it indeed becomes the giver of infinite fruit. || 76 ||
One should offer to Viṣṇu that which has been performed according to the injunctions;
likewise, one should offer to Him all those things abandoned due to prohibitions. || 77 ||
Therefore, for the sake of worshipping the Lord, one should not be intent on the acquisition of wealth;
therefore, Hari alone is the Great Compassionate One, and no other. (78)
Whatever is to be enjoyed in the three abodes and whoever is proclaimed as the enjoyer—he who knows both of these, while enjoying, is not defiled. (79)

"The enjoyment [of the food] shall be of a different nature, inconceivable even by the gods"—thus one should recollect such verses as these, according to one's ability, while eating the food of Hari. 80.

Human beings according to their division by caste (varṇa) and likewise by their division by stage of life (āśrama), as well as kings, human-gandharvas, gods, and the long-lived ancestors (pitṛs). || 81 ||
Those born of the womb and those born of their own nature, such as Jaya and others, Sanaka and others, Puṣkara, the remaining gods, Śani, Uṣā, and likewise Budha. (82)
Likewise Svāhā, Parjanya, Manu, Vāyujā, Vighneśvara, Mitra, Vasiṣṭha, Agni, and Nārada. || 83 ||
Varuṇa, Vidhu, Pravaha, Aniruddha, Taijasa, Indra, Agni, Mitravindā, Rudra, Vāṇī, and Māruta; || 84 ||
These, however, are objects of devotion to the Blessed One in an ascending order;
seekers of liberation should constantly practice devotion toward them in due sequence. (85)
Indeed, all these are always the gurus of a person; therefore, they are to be honored, saluted, and meditated upon on all sides of Hari. 86.
Even though Hari is equal and possesses equal qualities toward all beings from Umā down to the Maruts,
when meditated upon, he bestows joy that increases more and more at each successive stage.
When Hari is worshipped through the distinctions among these deities, from Nāma down to Māruta, He bestows liberation; there is no doubt in this matter.
Thus ends the tenth chapter of the *Yogadīpikā*.
Thus the *Yogadīpikā*, composed by Nārāyaṇa Paṇḍitācārya, son of the venerable Trivikrama Paṇḍitācārya— the ornament of the assembly of poets, is complete.
May the illustrious Lakṣmī-Veṅkaṭeśa be gracious.
May this be offered unto Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
